posts.summaryHtml: The six lowest states of a particle in a square box, from random starting vectors, in 103 steps of LOBPCG, and the 576 by 576 Hamiltonian is never written down. Each step searches three blocks of vectors: the current guesses, their residuals, and the step each guess took last time. Leave out the third block and the same run takes 797 steps.
posts.summaryText: The six lowest states of a particle in a square box, from random starting vectors, in 103 steps of LOBPCG, and the 576 by 576 Hamiltonian is never written down. Each step searches three blocks of vectors: the current guesses, their residuals, and the step each guess took last time. Leave out the third block and the same run takes 797 steps.
notes: ## The problem

A particle in a square box of side 1, with ℏ=m=1, has the Hamiltonian H=−21​∇2 and ψ=0 on the walls. Put it on a grid of 24 by 24 interior points, spacing h=1/25, and the Laplacian becomes the five-point stencil: at each point, four times the value there minus the four neighbors, over h2. The grid Hamiltonian is then a symmetric matrix with 576 rows. Its eigenvalues are known exactly, so every number the solver produces can be checked. The mode with j half-waves across and k down has energy
Ejk​=2h21​[(2−2cos25jπ​)+(2−2cos25kπ​)],
a little below the continuous box's π2(j2+k2)/2. We want the lowest six: (1,1), then (1,2) and (2,1), which have the same energy, then (2,2), then (1,3) and (3,1), again a pair.
## Why not diagonalize

eig_sym on the 576 by 576 matrix would return all 576 eigenpairs, and its cost grows as the cube of the size. We want six of them. Worse, the matrix has to exist: 5762 numbers, of which at most five per row are not zero. On a 3-D grid of 100 points a side it would have 1012 entries, 8 TB of doubles, while applying it to a vector touches seven numbers per point.

How do you find the lowest eigenvectors of H when the one thing you can do with it is compute Hx? In this program that is apply_box, a few whole-array shifts. In the plane-wave DFT code on this site it is two FFTs and a projector sum, and the difference is measured: silicon with the matrix built and diagonalized at every k-point takes several times as long as with this solver (the timings, native on one core, are in dft/README.md).
## A minimum instead of a factorization

The Rayleigh quotient of a vector is ρ(x)=xHHx/xHx. Write x in the eigenvectors of H, x=∑i​ci​vi​, and it becomes ∑i​∣ci​∣2λi​/∑i​∣ci​∣2: a weighted average of the eigenvalues. An average is smallest when all the weight sits on the smallest value, so the minimum of ρ over all vectors is λ1​, reached at the ground state. Finding the lowest eigenvector is therefore a minimization.

The gradient of ρ is 2(Hx−ρx)/xHx. The vector r=Hx−ρx is the residual: it is zero exactly when x is an eigenvector, and its norm bounds how far ρ is from the nearest eigenvalue. So the direction downhill costs one application of H, and the residual's norm tells you when to stop.

For the lowest several states, carry several vectors at once, kept orthonormal. The lowest k eigenvalues are what the k Rayleigh quotients add up to at the minimum, and the k vectors that reach it span the lowest k eigenvectors.
## Three blocks

Steepest descent would move each vector along its residual, x−αr, with α chosen to make ρ as small as possible. Choosing that α is itself a small eigenvalue problem. For any set of orthonormal vectors S (as rows), the best combinations of them are found by forming the small matrix S∗HST and diagonalizing it; its eigenvalues are the lowest Rayleigh quotients available in the span of S (Ritz values) and its eigenvectors say which combinations reach them (Ritz vectors). This is called Rayleigh-Ritz. With S=[x;r] the best α comes out of a 2 by 2.
LOBPCG searches a bigger span. Each step it takes the lowest Ritz vectors of three blocks stacked together:
- x, the current approximations, - w, their residuals, made orthogonal to x and scaled to unit length, and - p, the step each approximation took the last time.

The third block is the conjugate-gradient idea. Steepest descent on a long, narrow valley zigzags from wall to wall, because each new step undoes part of the last one. Keeping the last step in the search space lets the method combine the two, and the combination points along the valley. "Locally optimal" means that instead of a formula for the step it takes the best point in the span of all three.

Here each block has eight rows, six wanted and two spare, so the eigenproblems a step solves are at most 24 by 24, cheap next to anything done to the full vectors. The spares are there because the highest vectors in a block converge slowest: nothing above them in the block keeps them separated from the rest of the spectrum. Degenerate pairs need no special treatment: any combination of (1,2) and (2,1) is an eigenvector with the same energy, and the block converges to some orthonormal pair spanning that plane.

The P in the name is for preconditioner: replace r by an approximation to (H−λ)−1r, which points closer to the correction needed. The DFT engine uses one built from the kinetic energy. This run uses none, so the figure is about the three blocks alone.
## Locking

A state whose residual norm is under the tolerance (10−8 here) is locked: its residual is left out of w, so no direction is spent pushing it further. It stays in the Rayleigh-Ritz step, though, so it still improves from the other states' directions. By then its residual is mostly rounding error, and adding it to the search space only makes the space more nearly dependent, the usual way LOBPCG runs into trouble (the notes in lib/lobpcg have the details).
[figure]
## What the run shows

The ground state is the first under 10−8, at step 75, and it keeps going down while locked, to 10−9.2 by the end. The two highest wanted states, (1,3) and (3,1), are the last, at steps 102 and 103, and the run stops there. Every level then agrees with the formula above to 3×10−13 (LEVEL_ERROR).

The eigenvalues get good much sooner than the vectors do. At step 50 the worst residual norm is 10−2.2 and the worst eigenvalue error is 10−6.9. That is because ρ is flat at an eigenvector: an error ϵ in the vector moves the Rayleigh quotient by about ϵ2.

Run the same iteration without p, which converge does by telling every step it is the first, and it is block steepest descent. From the same starting vectors it needs 797 steps to meet the same tolerance.

The levels also sit where they should relative to the continuous box. The five-point stencil drops the h2 term of the second derivative's Taylor series, which lowers each level by about h2π4(j4+k4)/24; the measured shifts match that to within half a percent.

from lobpcg import (
    lobpcg, LOBPCG_HX, lobpcg_start, lobpcg_step, LOBPCG_X, no_preconditioner, random_rows,
    rayleigh_quotients, residuals, row_norms,
)

#: M  grid points along each side of the box
M = 24
#: SPACING  distance between grid points in a box of side 1, whose walls are
#:     the points just outside the grid
SPACING = 1.0 / (M + 1.0)
#: BLOCK  vectors carried at once: the six states wanted and two more
BLOCK = 8
#: WANTED  states that must converge
WANTED = 6
#: TOL  the residual norm a wanted state must get under
TOL = 1.0e-8
#: DIM  rows of the grid Hamiltonian, one per grid point
DIM = M * M
#: ENTRIES  the numbers a dense DIM by DIM matrix would store; the program never builds it
ENTRIES = DIM * DIM
#: SIDE_3D  for comparison, a 3-D grid this many points a side
SIDE_3D = 100.0
#: ENTRIES_3D  the entries of that grid's dense Hamiltonian, (SIDE_3D^3)^2
ENTRIES_3D = pow(SIDE_3D, 6.0)
pi = 4.0 * atan(1.0)

# A state is M*M numbers, the grid stored row after row, so point (i, j) is
# entry i*M + j. These masks are 1 where a point has a neighbor on that side
# inside the box and 0 where that neighbor is the wall, where psi = 0. They
# are the shape of a whole block, because arrays multiply only shape to shape.
HAS_LEFT = zeros(BLOCK, M * M)
HAS_RIGHT = zeros(BLOCK, M * M)
HAS_UP = zeros(BLOCK, M * M)
HAS_DOWN = zeros(BLOCK, M * M)
for b to BLOCK {
    for i to M {
        for j to M {
            if j > 0 {
                HAS_LEFT[b, i * M + j] = 1.0
            }
            if j < M - 1 {
                HAS_RIGHT[b, i * M + j] = 1.0
            }
            if i > 0 {
                HAS_UP[b, i * M + j] = 1.0
            }
            if i < M - 1 {
                HAS_DOWN[b, i * M + j] = 1.0
            }
        }
    }
}

#| $-\frac12 \nabla^2 \psi$ on the grid, for each row of a real block: the
#| five-point stencil $(4\psi_{ij} - \psi_{i\pm1,j} - \psi_{i,j\pm1}) / 2h^2$.
#| `roll` along the row brings each point's neighbor to it; the masks zero the
#| neighbors that fall outside the box.
def kinetic_real(psi) {
    left = roll(psi, 1, 1) * HAS_LEFT
    right = roll(psi, -1, 1) * HAS_RIGHT
    up = roll(psi, M, 1) * HAS_UP
    down = roll(psi, -M, 1) * HAS_DOWN
    return (4.0 * psi - left - right - up - down) / (2.0 * SPACING * SPACING)
}

#| The Hamiltonian of a particle in a box, applied to each row of `x`. It is
#| real, so it acts on the real and imaginary parts separately.
def apply_box(x) {
    return complex(kinetic_real(re(x)), kinetic_real(im(x)))
}

#| The exact eigenvalue of the grid Hamiltonian for the mode with j and k
#| half-waves: a sum of two 1-D second-difference eigenvalues.
def grid_level(j, k) {
    one_d_j = (2.0 - 2.0 * cos(j * pi / (M + 1.0))) / (2.0 * SPACING * SPACING)
    one_d_k = (2.0 - 2.0 * cos(k * pi / (M + 1.0))) / (2.0 * SPACING * SPACING)
    return one_d_j + one_d_k
}

#| The level of the same mode in the continuous box, $\pi^2 (j^2 + k^2) / 2$.
def box_level(j, k) {
    return pi * pi * (j * j + k * k) / 2.0
}

#: MODE_J, MODE_K  the six lowest modes (j, k), lowest first
MODE_J = [1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3]
MODE_K = [1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]
EXACT = zeros(WANTED)
for s to WANTED {
    EXACT[s] = grid_level(MODE_J[s], MODE_K[s])
}

#| Run LOBPCG a step at a time from the rows of `start`, recording each wanted
#| state's residual norm (log10) and eigenvalue error (log10) per step in
#| `residual_log` and `error_log`. With `use_previous_step` false every step is
#| taken as step 0, which never searches along p: that is block steepest
#| descent. Returns the number of steps taken to converge, or `max_steps`.
def converge(start, max_steps, use_previous_step, residual_log, error_log) {
    state = lobpcg_start(apply_box, start)
    for step to max_steps {
        x = slab(state, LOBPCG_X)
        hx = slab(state, LOBPCG_HX)
        lam = rayleigh_quotients(x, hx)
        norms = row_norms(residuals(x, hx, lam))
        for s to WANTED {
            residual_log[s, step] = log(max(norms[s], 1.0e-300)) / log(10.0)
            error_log[s, step] = log(max(abs(lam[s] - EXACT[s]), 1.0e-300)) / log(10.0)
        }
        as_step = 0
        if use_previous_step {
            as_step = step
        }
        worst = lobpcg_step(apply_box, no_preconditioner, state, as_step, WANTED, TOL)
        if worst < TOL {
            return step
        }
    }
    return max_steps
}

MAX_STEPS = 1000
srand(1.0)
START = random_rows(BLOCK, M * M)
RESIDUAL_LOG = zeros(WANTED, MAX_STEPS)
ERROR_LOG = zeros(WANTED, MAX_STEPS)
STEPS = converge(START, MAX_STEPS, true, RESIDUAL_LOG, ERROR_LOG)
SD_RESIDUAL_LOG = zeros(WANTED, MAX_STEPS)
SD_ERROR_LOG = zeros(WANTED, MAX_STEPS)
SD_STEPS = converge(START, MAX_STEPS, false, SD_RESIDUAL_LOG, SD_ERROR_LOG)
show STEPS
show SD_STEPS

# the answer, from the library's own driver, from other random vectors
VECTORS = random_rows(BLOCK, M * M)
LEVELS = zeros(BLOCK)
WORST = lobpcg(apply_box, no_preconditioner, VECTORS, LEVELS, MAX_STEPS, WANTED, TOL)
show WORST
WANTED_LEVELS = zeros(WANTED)
for s to WANTED {
    WANTED_LEVELS[s] = LEVELS[s]
}
show WANTED_LEVELS
show EXACT
# the worst difference between a level and the grid's exact level
LEVEL_ERROR = max(abs(WANTED_LEVELS - EXACT))
show LEVEL_ERROR

#| Row `s` of a per-step log, its first `n` entries.
def history(log, s, n) {
    row = zeros(n)
    for t to n {
        row[t] = log[s, t]
    }
    return row
}

#| The largest entry of each column of a per-step log, its first `n` columns:
#| the worst of the wanted states at each step.
def worst_per_step(log, n) {
    row = zeros(n)
    for t to n {
        row[t] = log[0, t]
        for s to WANTED {
            row[t] = max(row[t], log[s, t])
        }
    }
    return row
}

STEP_AXIS = zeros(STEPS + 1)
for t to STEPS + 1 {
    STEP_AXIS[t] = t
}
figure("Residual norm of each state, per LOBPCG step", "step", "$\\log_{10} \\|Hx - \\lambda x\\|$", 0.0, STEPS, -10.0, 3.0)
plot(STEP_AXIS, history(RESIDUAL_LOG, 0, STEPS + 1), "(1,1)")
plot(STEP_AXIS, history(RESIDUAL_LOG, 1, STEPS + 1), "(1,2)")
plot(STEP_AXIS, history(RESIDUAL_LOG, 2, STEPS + 1), "(2,1)")
plot(STEP_AXIS, history(RESIDUAL_LOG, 3, STEPS + 1), "(2,2)")
plot(STEP_AXIS, history(RESIDUAL_LOG, 4, STEPS + 1), "(1,3)")
plot(STEP_AXIS, history(RESIDUAL_LOG, 5, STEPS + 1), "(3,1)")
plot(STEP_AXIS, zeros(STEPS + 1) + log(TOL) / log(10.0), "tolerance")

# every fifth step, which is plenty for a line this smooth
SD_POINTS = floor(SD_STEPS / 5.0) + 1
SD_AXIS = zeros(SD_POINTS)
SD_WORST = zeros(SD_POINTS)
LOBPCG_WORST = zeros(SD_POINTS)
SD_ALL = worst_per_step(SD_RESIDUAL_LOG, SD_STEPS + 1)
LOBPCG_ALL = worst_per_step(RESIDUAL_LOG, STEPS + 1)
for t to SD_POINTS {
    SD_AXIS[t] = 5.0 * t
    SD_WORST[t] = SD_ALL[5 * t]
    LOBPCG_WORST[t] = LOBPCG_ALL[min(5 * t, STEPS)]
}
figure("The worst wanted residual, with and without the previous step p", "step", "$\\log_{10}$ residual norm", 0.0, SD_STEPS, -9.0, 3.0)
plot(SD_AXIS, LOBPCG_WORST, "LOBPCG: x, w and p (held at its last value once done)")
plot(SD_AXIS, SD_WORST, "steepest descent: x and w")

# the six states, one panel each: the sign of each is arbitrary, and a
# degenerate pair comes out as some orthonormal pair in its plane
#| State `s` as an M by M picture: row i, column j is the grid point (i, j).
def state_picture(s) {
    picture = zeros(M, M)
    for i to M {
        for j to M {
            picture[i, j] = re(VECTORS[s, i * M + j])
        }
    }
    return picture
}
# one color scale for all six: white at zero, the same red and blue for the same size
PSI_MAX = 0.0
for s to WANTED {
    PSI_MAX = max(PSI_MAX, max(abs(state_picture(s))))
}
grid("The six lowest states", 2, 3)
figure("(1,1)", "", "")
plot2d(state_picture(0), "$\\psi$")
colormap("diverging")
clim(-PSI_MAX, PSI_MAX)
figure("the (1,2) and (2,1) pair", "", "")
plot2d(state_picture(1), "$\\psi$")
colormap("diverging")
clim(-PSI_MAX, PSI_MAX)
figure("the (1,2) and (2,1) pair", "", "")
plot2d(state_picture(2), "$\\psi$")
colormap("diverging")
clim(-PSI_MAX, PSI_MAX)
figure("(2,2)", "", "")
plot2d(state_picture(3), "$\\psi$")
colormap("diverging")
clim(-PSI_MAX, PSI_MAX)
figure("the (1,3) and (3,1) pair", "", "")
plot2d(state_picture(4), "$\\psi$")
colormap("diverging")
clim(-PSI_MAX, PSI_MAX)
figure("the (1,3) and (3,1) pair", "", "")
plot2d(state_picture(5), "$\\psi$")
colormap("diverging")
clim(-PSI_MAX, PSI_MAX)

test "the six lowest levels are the grid's exact levels, to 1e-12" {
    assert_lt(WORST, TOL)
    for s to WANTED {
        assert_near(LEVELS[s], EXACT[s], 1.0e-12)
    }
}

test "every level agrees with the formula to 3e-13" {
    # measured 2.27e-13: rounding in levels of size 10 to 50
    assert_lt(LEVEL_ERROR, 3.0e-13)
}
test "each degenerate pair comes out degenerate" {
    assert_near(LEVELS[1], LEVELS[2], 1.0e-12)
    assert_near(LEVELS[4], LEVELS[5], 1.0e-12)
    assert_lt(1.0, LEVELS[3] - LEVELS[2])
}

test "at step 50 the eigenvalue error is under the square of the residual norm" {
    worst_residual = worst_per_step(RESIDUAL_LOG, 51)
    worst_error = worst_per_step(ERROR_LOG, 51)
    # both are log10
    assert_lt(worst_error[50], 2.0 * worst_residual[50])
}

test "without p it is block steepest descent, and takes more than seven times as many steps" {
    # the counts the prose quotes, the same in every engine
    assert_near(STEPS, 103, 0.0)
    assert_near(SD_STEPS, 797, 0.0)
    assert_lt(7.0 * STEPS, SD_STEPS)
    assert_lt(SD_STEPS, MAX_STEPS)
}

test "the grid levels sit below the box's by h^2 pi^4 (j^4 + k^4) / 24, to 1%" {
    for s to WANTED {
        j = MODE_J[s]
        k = MODE_K[s]
        predicted = SPACING * SPACING * pi * pi * pi * pi * (j * j * j * j + k * k * k * k) / 24.0
        assert_near(box_level(j, k) - LEVELS[s], predicted, 0.01 * predicted)
    }
}

functions.name: inverse
functions.what: The inverse of `M`, column by column against the identity.

functions.name: test_matrix
functions.what: An `n` by `n` matrix whose entries are a fixed, ugly, reproducible mess in the range -1 to 1. The same `seed` always gives the same matrix.

functions.name: reflect
functions.what: Apply the Householder reflector built from `v` to the window of `m` rows and columns starting at `p`: `H` from both sides, so its eigenvalues do not move, and `Q` from the right, so that `A = Q H Q^T` still holds afterwards.  The two ranges are not an optimization. From the left it touches columns `c0` and rightwards, and from the right it touches rows `r1` and upwards, because everything outside those is already zero and must stay zero -- a reflector applied to the whole row would write dust back into a subdiagonal entry that deflation had just decided was negligible, and the factor would never finish being quasi-triangular.

functions.name: rotate
functions.what: Apply the plane rotation `[[cs, -sn], [sn, cs]]` on rows and columns `k` and `k + 1` the same way: `T` from both sides, `Q` from the right.  This is only ever called on a block that has already deflated, so everything left of column `k` in those two rows, and everything below row `k + 1` in those two columns, is zero. It stays out of both. A sweep leaves dust of order 1e-17 below the subdiagonal where exact arithmetic leaves zeros, and a rotation over the full row would mix that dust straight into the subdiagonal entry deflation had just set to zero, turning a converged 2 by 2 into two blocks that no longer look converged.

functions.name: hessenberg
functions.what: Reduce `A` to upper Hessenberg form. Fills `H` and `Q` so that `A = Q H Q^T`, `Q^T Q = I`, and `H[i, j] = 0` whenever `i > j + 1`. One reflection per column, each one zeroing everything below the subdiagonal of that column and leaving the columns already done alone.

functions.name: francis_step
functions.what: One implicit double-shift QR sweep over the unreduced Hessenberg block from `lo` to `hi`, for a pair of shifts given by their sum `s` and product `t`. The shifts are never formed: the first reflector is built from the first column of `(H - s1)(H - s2)`, which expands to something needing only `s` and `t`, and that is what "implicit" means. The rest of the sweep chases the resulting bulge back down to Hessenberg form.

functions.name: split2
functions.what: Put the 2 by 2 block at `k` into standard form. If its two eigenvalues are real it is made upper triangular, which splits it into two 1 by 1 blocks and returns 1.0. If they are a complex pair the two diagonal entries are rotated until they are equal, which is the form a real Schur factor is supposed to have, and it returns 0.0.

functions.name: schur_norm
functions.what: The Frobenius norm, used as the yardstick a subdiagonal entry is called negligible against when its two diagonal neighbors are both zero.

functions.name: schur_advance
functions.what: One step of the outer iteration on the block ending at `hi`, and the whole of what the driver does per turn: walk up from `hi` to the first negligible subdiagonal entry, then either deflate what is below it or sweep it. Returns the new `hi`, which is unchanged exactly when a sweep happened.  `its` is how many sweeps have already been spent here without deflating. A sweep that keeps landing in the same place is stalling on a shift that is useless for this matrix, so every tenth one throws an arbitrary shift of the right size at it instead. The constants are the ones LAPACK settled on.

functions.name: schur
functions.what: The real Schur decomposition. Fills `T` and `Q` so that `A = Q T Q^T` with `Q` orthogonal and `T` quasi-triangular. Reduce to Hessenberg once, then sweep and deflate from the bottom right until nothing is left.

functions.name: schur_blocks
functions.what: Where each diagonal block starts, written into `starts`, and how many there are, returned. A 2 by 2 block is one entry, not two: `T[k + 1, k]` is nonzero exactly when `k` heads a 2 by 2.

functions.name: schur_block_re
functions.what: The real part of the eigenvalues of the block starting at `k`. Both of them for a 2 by 2, and both are the same number there, because `split2` made the diagonal entries equal.

functions.name: schur_residual
functions.what: How far `A - Q T Q^T` is from zero, entry by entry: the decomposition's own certificate, and the number to look at before believing anything downstream.

functions.name: orthogonality
functions.what: How far `Q^T Q` is from the identity.

functions.name: sylvester_small
functions.what: Solve `T11 X - X T22 = C`, where `T11` and `T22` are the two adjacent diagonal blocks at `k`, by writing the whole thing out as one linear system in the entries of `X`. With both blocks of size 1 or 2 that system has at most four unknowns, so there is no reason to be clever about it. It is singular exactly when the two blocks share an eigenvalue, which is the one case where the two cannot be swapped.

functions.name: orth_basis
functions.what: Householder QR of the `m` by `p` matrix `V`, throwing away the triangular factor and keeping the orthogonal one: fills `Z` with an `m` by `m` orthogonal matrix whose first `p` columns span the same space `V`'s do. `V` is overwritten.

functions.name: apply_block
functions.what: Apply the small orthogonal `Z` as a similarity on the window of `m` rows and columns starting at `k`, and on `Q` from the right. Same reasoning about ranges as `reflect`: outside the window everything is already zero.

functions.name: swap_blocks
functions.what: Exchange the two adjacent diagonal blocks at `k`, of sizes `n1` then `n2`, so that afterwards `n2` comes first. The eigenvalues do not change; only where they sit on the diagonal does, and `Q` follows.  The trick is that the columns of `[X; I]` span the invariant subspace of the trailing block, where `X` solves `T11 X - X T22 = -T12`. An orthonormal basis for that span, completed to a square orthogonal matrix, is the swap.

functions.name: block_size
functions.what: The size of the diagonal block starting at `k`: 2 if it heads a 2 by 2, else 1.

functions.name: reorder_stable
functions.what: Move every block whose eigenvalues have a negative real part to the top left, in the order they already appear, and return how many rows they take up. That leading corner of `Q` is then an orthonormal basis for the stable invariant subspace, which is what the Riccati solver needs.

functions.name: svd_jacobi
functions.what: Decompose `A`, which is `m` by `n` with `m >= n`. `A` is overwritten with `U S`, so its columns come back scaled by the singular values; `s` gets the singular values and `V` the right vectors, in whatever order the sweeps left them. Returns how many sweeps it took.

functions.name: svd
functions.what: The full decomposition, sorted: `U` is `m` by `n`, `s` descends, and `A = U diag(s) V^T`. `A` is left alone.

functions.name: svd_residual
functions.what: The largest entry of `A - U diag(s) V^T`.

functions.name: svd_orthonormal
functions.what: How far the `n` columns of an `m` by `n` matrix are from orthonormal.

functions.name: svd_with_values
functions.what: A matrix with the singular values you ask for: `Q1 diag(want) Q2^T`, with the two orthogonal factors taken from the Schur vectors of two unrelated matrices, so nothing about the construction lines up with the axes.

functions.name: input_shape
functions.what: The inputs' shape: a matrix `S` whose singular values fall evenly on a log scale from 1 to 0.01, so the loudest input direction is a hundred times the quietest. The loss is `f(W) = |(W - W*) S|^2 / 2`; its gradient is `(W - W*) S S^T`, and `S S^T` has eigenvalues from 1 down to `1e-4`.

functions.name: race_layout
functions.what: The model is one tensor, the map `W`.

functions.name: loss
functions.what: The training loss at `theta`.

functions.name: miss
functions.what: How far `theta` is from the true map, in the Frobenius norm: how much of the map is still wrong, counting every direction the same whatever its input size.

functions.name: gradient
functions.what: The gradient of the loss, written into `grad`.

functions.name: quietest_direction
functions.what: The quietest input direction: the eigenvector of `S S^T` with the smallest eigenvalue, `1e-4`. The loss barely depends on what `W` does to it.

functions.name: quiet_left
functions.what: How much of the error along the quietest direction is left: `|(W - W*) v|` over its value at the start, `|W* v|`.

functions.name: race
functions.what: Run `opt` from `start` for `STEPS` steps, starting at step size `lr` and decaying it in a straight line to zero. `curve[step]` records the miss before each step and after the last. Returns the parameters it ends at.

posts.title: Muon orthogonalizes the update
posts.titleHtml: Muon orthogonalizes the update
posts.titleText: Muon orthogonalizes the update
posts.summaryHtml: Muon is an optimizer that keeps the directions of a gradient matrix and gives every one of them a step of about the same size, however lopsided the gradient is. Five Newton-Schulz steps get close to that without an SVD. On a problem whose inputs differ in size a hundredfold, it ends at least 4.5 times closer to the answer than SGD, momentum or Adam at their best step sizes, and behind momentum in training loss.
posts.summaryText: Muon is an optimizer that keeps the directions of a gradient matrix and gives every one of them a step of about the same size, however lopsided the gradient is. Five Newton-Schulz steps get close to that without an SVD. On a problem whose inputs differ in size a hundredfold, it ends at least 4.5 times closer to the answer than SGD, momentum or Adam at their best step sizes, and behind momentum in training loss.
notes: ## The problem it solves

A weight matrix W maps inputs to outputs. Training moves it against the gradient G, the matrix of how fast the loss changes with each entry of W. Plain gradient descent (SGD) takes the step −ηG, where η, the learning rate, is a step size chosen by hand.

Every matrix can be written G=USVT, its singular value decomposition. The columns of V are input directions, the columns of U are output directions, and the singular values on the diagonal of S say how hard the gradient pushes along each pair. An SGD step moves W along each pair by η times that pair's singular value. When the singular values are lopsided, the few large ones get nearly all of the movement and the small ones almost none.

The problem here is built to show that. It learns an 8 by 8 linear map W∗ from inputs whose size in different directions spans a factor of a hundred, with loss 21​∥(W−W∗)Sin​∥2. The gradient is (W−W∗)Sin​SinT​, and Sin​SinT​ has eigenvalues from 1 down to 10−4. The first gradient's singular values run from 2.04 down to 3.5×10−5, a factor of 57,000. A direction the inputs barely excite gets a gradient ten thousand times weaker than the loudest one, and SGD's step along it is ten thousand times shorter.

Muon keeps the directions and drops the singular values: it steps along UVT, which moves W by the same amount along every pair. That is what orthogonalizing the update means, since UVT has orthonormal rows and every singular value equal to 1. Adam does something like it one entry of W at a time, dividing each entry's step by that entry's recent gradient size. Muon does it one direction of the matrix at a time, and those directions need not line up with the entries.
## Newton-Schulz, without an SVD

Muon does not compute U and V. It divides G by its Frobenius norm (the square root of the sum of the squares of its entries), which puts every singular value in (0,1], and then applies a matrix polynomial five times:
X←aX+b(XXT)X+c(XXT)2X,(a,b,c)=(3.4445,−4.775,2.0315)

Since XXT=US2UT, one step turns USVT into Up(S)VT, where p(s)=as+bs3+cs5 is applied to each singular value separately. The directions never move. Two tests check this: the singular values after five steps match, to nine digits, p applied five times to the ones before; and GT times the result is symmetric with positive eigenvalues, which holds when the two share their singular vectors.
[figure]

The coefficients were tuned for speed near zero. p′(0)=3.4445, so a small singular value grows about 3.4445 times per step. The price is that 1 is not a fixed point: iterated, the values settle into a band between 0.68 and 1.14 and keep moving inside it (lib/polar measures the band). On the first gradient here, the singular values after dividing by the norm are
and after five steps they are

The five largest are in the band. The three smallest have grown by as much as 484.87 times, close to 3.44455=484.88, and are still below it. So Muon's step is not exactly UVT. Its directions are right and its sizes are much more even than the gradient's, and the next steps keep working on what is left.
## Momentum and the step size

Muon orthogonalizes a momentum built from the gradients. It keeps M←μM+G, a running sum of gradients that shrinks by the factor μ (0.9 here) every step, and steps W←W−ηNS(M), where NS is the five Newton-Schulz steps. The length of that step is set by η and not by the gradient, so near the minimum it does not get shorter by itself. The step size has to shrink instead: every optimizer in the race starts at its own η and lowers it in a straight line to zero over the run.
## The race

SGD, SGD with momentum, Adam and Muon each take 100 steps from W=0. Each gets its best starting step size from the same grid, 0.01 * 2^g for g = 0, ..., 10, judged by how far it ends from the true map in the Frobenius norm. They start 4.96 away, and they end:

SGD                 2.74    (step size 2.56)
SGD with momentum   1.64    (2.56)
Adam                2.63    (0.64)
Muon                0.26 to 0.36    (0.64)

Muon's entry is a range because its result depends on rounding. The program runs Muon and momentum again from eight more starts, each W=0 with one entry moved by 10−12, about the rounding error of one multiplication. Momentum's result moves by less than 10−13. Muon's moves by up to a tenth: 0.26 to 0.36 over those nine starts, whether the program runs natively or in a browser. Newton-Schulz enlarges a small singular value by up to about 485 times, whatever put it there, and a rounding error in the momentum is no exception.

Even at the worst of the nine, Muon ends 4.5 times closer than the best of the others. The quietest input direction shows why. Along it SGD multiplies the error by 1−10−4η each step, and after 100 steps 98.7% of the error is still there; a test computes that product and matches the run to twelve digits. Momentum leaves 89.6%. Muon leaves between 11% and 29%.

Measured by training loss instead, Muon is behind. From 2.67, momentum ends at 4.2×10−4 from every start, and Muon ends above that in eight of the nine runs, as high as 2.9×10−3; the ninth ends just below, at 4.20×10−4 against 4.23×10−4. The quiet directions are the ones the loss hardly counts, so an optimizer can leave them alone and still reach a low loss. Getting them right matters once the model sees inputs that point along them more than the training inputs did.
The optimizers are in lib/optim, over the parameter layout of lib/params, and the Newton-Schulz iteration is in lib/polar. The transformer post in this channel trains with the same muon step.

posts.summaryHtml: A copy of the doubling-time post that adds the rule of 72. Above a rate of 4.90% a year it is closer to the exact doubling time than the rule of 70, and below that the rule of 70 is closer; at 8% the rule of 72 is off by 0.07%. The original four tests are kept word for word.
posts.summaryText: A copy of the doubling-time post that adds the rule of 72. Above a rate of 4.90% a year it is closer to the exact doubling time than the rule of 70, and below that the rule of 70 is closer; at 8% the rule of 72 is off by 0.07%. The original four tests are kept word for word.
notes: The site checks that the original's tests are here unchanged and still pass, and that the tests below them are new.

Both rules approximate ln2/ln(1+r). Expanding the logarithm one more term gives t≈100r69.3​(1+2r​), so the exact time, multiplied by 100r, is not a constant: it is 69.3 plus about 35r. At 3% that is 70.3, and 70 is the closer rule; at 8% it is 72.1, and 72 is. The program finds the rate where the two rules are equally far off by bisection: 4.90%.

functions.name: basis_rows
functions.what: A flat row-major vector as rows of `width` columns.

functions.name: basis_of
functions.what: The record from the two flat vectors a generated module holds.

functions.name: basis_first
functions.what: The first shell row of element `z`, or `-1` when the set has none for it.

functions.name: basis_count
functions.what: How many shells element `z` has.

functions.name: basis_nao
functions.what: `[Cartesian AOs, spherical AOs]` of one atom of element `z`.

functions.name: basis_check
functions.what: The number of ways the table breaks its own layout: an element's shells not in one run, elements out of order, a primitive row skipped or used twice, an exponent that is not positive. `0` for a good table.

functions.name: bas_ncart
functions.what: Cartesian components in a shell of angular momentum `l`.

functions.name: bas_nsph
functions.what: Spherical components in a shell of angular momentum `l`.

functions.name: bas_odfact
functions.what: The odd double factorial `(2k-1)!!`, with `(-1)!! = 1`.

functions.name: bas_powers
functions.what: The powers of every Cartesian component of a shell, `[ncart, 3]`, in PySCF's order.

functions.name: bas_fc
functions.what: The factor between PySCF's Cartesian component and the unit one: PySCF = unit * F. It is one for s and p [test "F squared matches PySCF's int1e_ovlp_cart diagonal for xx and xy"].

functions.name: bas_nc
functions.what: The component factor `Nc`: it cancels the double factorials of the Gaussian moments, so `cn` can be shared by every component of a shell.

functions.name: bas_nr
functions.what: The radial norm `Nr(a, l) = (2a/pi)^(3/4) (4a)^(l/2)`.

functions.name: bas_prim_overlap
functions.what: Overlap of two unit primitives of one shell with exponents `a` and `b`.

functions.name: shell_atom
functions.what: The atom shell `s` sits on.

functions.name: shell_l
functions.what: The angular momentum of shell `s`.

functions.name: shell_cart0
functions.what: The index of shell `s`'s first Cartesian basis function.

functions.name: shell_sph0
functions.what: The index of shell `s`'s first spherical basis function.

functions.name: shell_nprim
functions.what: The number of primitives of shell `s`.

functions.name: shell_p0
functions.what: The row of shell `s`'s first primitive in the primitives table.

functions.name: shell_f0
functions.what: The index of shell `s`'s first basis function: spherical when `sph = 1`, Cartesian otherwise.

functions.name: bas_atom_pos
functions.what: The position of atom `a`, `[x, y, z]` in bohr.

functions.name: bas_prim_exp
functions.what: The exponent of primitive `p`.

functions.name: bas_nao_cart
functions.what: Cartesian AO count of a shell pack.

functions.name: bas_nao_sph
functions.what: Spherical AO count of a shell pack.

functions.name: bas_ao_table
functions.what: One row per Cartesian AO: (shell, atom, lx, ly, lz), `[nao_cart, 5]`. Rows follow the shells in order and the components in PySCF's order, which is what `SH_CART0` counts.

functions.name: bas_contract
functions.what: Contracted coefficients `cn[nprimtot]` in the unit-Cartesian convention: raw coefficient times `Nr(a_p, l)`, with the shell rescaled to contracted self-overlap one [test "16 seeded shells up to f come out with unit self-overlap in every component"].

functions.name: bas_rng
functions.what: Test helper: the next uniform number in `(0, 1)` from a Park-Miller state held in `st[0]`, so a failing shell can be quoted by its seed.

functions.name: bas_moment_self_overlap
functions.what: Test helper: the self-overlap of component `(lx, ly, lz)` of shell `s`, summed from 1-D Gaussian moments, one axis at a time. It shares no formula with `bas_prim_overlap`.

functions.name: bas_random_shells
functions.what: Test helper: `nsh` random shells with `l < BAS_T_NL` (s to f), from one to `BAS_T_NPRIM_MAX` primitives each, exponents spread from $10^{-1.5}$ to $10^{3.5}$ and coefficients that are sometimes negative. Returns the shells and prims packs.

functions.name: molecule_bohr
functions.what: The molecule of atomic numbers `z[natm]` at `xyz[natm, 3]` (bohr), with every atom's shells from basis `b`: neutral, spin from the electron count's parity, spherical functions.

functions.name: molecule_from
functions.what: The molecule of atomic numbers `z[natm]` at `xyz[natm, 3]` in angstrom, with every atom's shells from basis `b`.

functions.name: molecule_packs
functions.what: A molecule from packs made elsewhere: neutral, spin from the parity, spherical functions.

functions.name: mol_nelectron
functions.what: The number of electrons.

functions.name: mol_nalpha
functions.what: Alpha electrons: `(N + spin) / 2`.

functions.name: mol_nbeta
functions.what: Beta electrons: `(N - spin) / 2`.

functions.name: mol_enuc
functions.what: The repulsion between the nuclei, `sum over pairs Z_A Z_B / R_AB`. A ghost atom (`Z = 0`) adds nothing, as in PySCF.

functions.name: mol_lmax
functions.what: The highest angular momentum of the basis.

functions.name: mol_spherical
functions.what: `1` when the run uses spherical functions that differ from the Cartesian ones: `cart` is `0` and some shell has `l >= 2`. Up to p the two sets are the same functions in the same order, so nothing is transformed.

functions.name: mol_nao
functions.what: The number of basis functions the SCF sees.

functions.name: boys_series_one
functions.what: `F_n(x)` at one order from its series. The terms grow while `2x > 2n + 2k + 3` and shrink after, so the stop test only fires past the peak, and a fixed term count would be wrong at the top of the range.

functions.name: boys_switch
functions.what: The switch `x_n` for order `n`: at or above it `boys_asym_up` is exact to rounding in every order up to `n`. The list is checked, value by value, against mpmath by `tools/boys_reference.py` (see the header for the rule).

functions.name: boys_down
functions.what: `F_0 .. F_nmax` from `F_nmax = top`, by the downward step.

functions.name: boys_series_down
functions.what: Every order from `0` to `nmax`: the series at `nmax`, then downward.

functions.name: boys_asym_up
functions.what: `F_0 = sqrt(pi/x)/2` and upward with the `e^-x` term kept, at or above `boys_switch(nmax)`; the series below it.

functions.name: boys_values
functions.what: The production entry: whichever member is most accurate at this `x`.

functions.name: boys_gl_nodes
functions.what: Gauss-Legendre nodes and weights on `[-1, 1]`: `GL[0, i]` is a node and `GL[1, i]` its weight. Newton's method on `P_m` from the usual cosine guess; it converges quadratically, so a fixed `BOYS_GL_NEWTON_IT` steps is past the point where the nodes stop moving.

functions.name: boys_gl_pass
functions.what: All orders at once on `npan` equal panels: one `exp` per node, then the powers `t^(2n)` by repeated multiplication.

functions.name: boys_quadrature
functions.what: Gauss-Legendre with the panel count doubled until every order agrees with the previous pass to `BOYS_QUAD_TOL` relative. At large `x` the integrand is a spike of width about `1/sqrt(x)` next to `t = 0` (for `n = 0`) or near `sqrt(n/x)`, which one panel cannot resolve; halving the panels resolves it within a few passes, and Gauss-Legendre converges fast once it is resolved, so the pass that meets the stop is at least as accurate as the stop [test "the series, the quadrature and the Taylor step each match mpmath to 1e-13"]. A stop at the size of the rounding noise between passes never fires: the doubling runs to `BOYS_QUAD_MAXPAN` panels, and the rounding of the long sum grows past the stop.

functions.name: boys_grid_range
functions.what: A Taylor grid for orders up to `ncap`, holding `npts` nodes from node index `i0` (node `i` sits at `x = i h`). Row `0` is a header `[h, i0, npts, ncap]`; row `r >= 1` holds `F_0 .. F_(ncap+K)` at node `i0 + r - 1`, the `K` extra orders being what the Taylor step needs.

functions.name: boys_grid_new
functions.what: The grid a caller builds once, for orders up to `nmax` and arguments up to `xmax`. It stops at the switch, because above it `boys_grid_eval` uses the asymptotic form, which is exact there and needs no table. The switch is taken at the highest order and over all orders below; the generator checks that `boys_switch` never falls with `n`, so that is the largest one.

functions.name: boys_grid_eval
functions.what: `F_0 .. F_nmax` at `x` from grid `G`. With `d = x - x0` for the nearest node `x0`, `F_nmax(x) = sum_k F_(nmax+k)(x0) (-d)^k / k!`, since `dF_n/dx = -F_(n+1)`. `|d| <= 0.05` and `F_(n+k) <= F_n`, so stopping at `k = 8` leaves at most `0.05^9 / 9! = 5.4e-18` of `F_nmax`. The lower orders then come downward. An `x` outside the grid, or an order above the one it was built for, falls back to the series, so a short grid is slow rather than wrong.

functions.name: boys_taylor
functions.what: The Taylor grid as a registry member: a one-node grid at the node nearest `x`, built on the spot. Slow, since it runs the series anyway, but it is the same evaluation code the per-caller grid uses.

functions.name: boys_methods
functions.what: The registry, production member first. Every member takes `(nmax, x)` and returns `F[0..nmax]`. Both parameters are numbers, as the frozen stage signature `(nmax, x) -> Arr` has them, and every member annotates them `: Num` and its result `-> Arr`, so the kinds are fixed in the member itself and not inferred from whichever call a program happens to make.

functions.name: herm_nh
functions.what: Hermite functions with `t + u + v <= L`.

functions.name: herm_tuv
functions.what: The Hermite index list for total order `L`, `[nh, 3]`: `t` counts up, then `u`, then `v`. Every table in this family uses this order.

functions.name: herm_esize
functions.what: Entries of a flat E table for one axis with powers up to `la` and `lb`.

functions.name: herm_efill
functions.what: Fill the flat 1-D table `E(i, j, t)`, `i <= la`, `j <= lb`, `t <= i + j`, into `E` from entry `e0` on, at `e0 + (i (lb + 1) + j) (la + lb + 1) + t`. `X` is `A - B` on this axis. The table is overwritten, so a caller can reuse one buffer for every primitive pair.

functions.name: herm_etab
functions.what: The frozen form: `E[la+1, lb+1, la+lb+1]` for exponents `a`, `b` and `XAB = A - B` on one axis.

functions.name: herm_rfill
functions.what: Fill `S[0 .. (L+1)^3)` with `pref * R(0; t, u, v)` at offset `(t (L+1) + u) (L+1) + v`, for `t + u + v <= L`. `S` needs `2 (L+1)^3` entries: the upper half is the scratch cube for odd `n`. `F` holds `F_0 .. F_L` at `alpha (X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2)`. Entries with `t + u + v > L` are left as they were, and nothing reads them.

functions.name: herm_rfill_box
functions.what: `pref * R(0; t, u, v)` for `t <= Tx`, `u <= Ty`, `v <= Tz` only, into `S` at `s0 + (t (Ty+1) + u) (Tz+1) + v`, using `2 (Tx+1)(Ty+1)(Tz+1)` entries from `s0` on. `F` holds `F_0 .. F_(Tx+Ty+Tz)`. This is what one integral needs: `(xx, xx | xx, xx)` has `Ty = Tz = 0`, so it builds one line of entries per level, where the full cube of the same order builds every entry with `t + u + v <= L`.

functions.name: herm_rtab
functions.what: The frozen form: `R[L+1, L+1, L+1]` with `R[t, u, v] = R(0; t, u, v)` for exponent `p`, `PC = P - C` and Boys values `F[0 .. L]` at `p |PC|^2`. Entries with `t + u + v > L` are zero.

functions.name: herm_grid
functions.what: A Boys grid for `herm_boys_fill`: `boys_grid_new(nmax, xmax)` with the switch of every order `n <= nmax` copied into its header row at column `BOYS_GRID_HDR + n` (the row is at least `nmax + 9` wide and `boys_grid_eval` reads only its first `BOYS_GRID_HDR` columns). `boys_switch` builds its list on every call, and an integral loop calls the fill once per primitive quartet.

functions.name: herm_boys_fill
functions.what: `F_0 .. F_nmax` at `x` into `F`, from a grid `G` built once by the caller with `herm_grid`. It is `boys_grid_eval` without the allocations: an integral loop calls it once per primitive quartet, and a fresh array each time would cost more than the Taylor step. Above the switch it is the asymptotic form with upward recursion, and an `x` or order the grid does not cover falls back to the series, exactly as in `lib/hf/boys`.

functions.name: herm_lambda
functions.what: Test helper: the Hermite Gaussian `d^t/dP^t exp(-p (x - P)^2)` at `x`, from the Hermite polynomial recursion. It shares no code with `herm_efill`.

functions.name: herm_overlap_1d
functions.what: Test helper: the 1-D overlap `int x_A^i x_B^j exp(-a x_A^2 - b x_B^2) dx` from the binomial expansion about `P` and the Gaussian moments. Another route to `E(i, j, 0) sqrt(pi/p)`.

functions.name: md1_grid
functions.what: The Boys grid a one-electron build needs: orders up to `2 lmax`.

functions.name: md1_pair
functions.what: S, T and V for shell pair `(sa, sb)`, as `[3, ncart_a * ncart_b]` with the component pair `(ia, ib)` at column `ia * ncart_b + ib`. `cn` comes from `bas_contract` and `G` from `md1_grid`.

functions.name: md1_all
functions.what: S, T and V for the whole basis, `[3, n, n]` over Cartesian AOs. Each shell pair is computed once, for `sa >= sb`, and mirrored, so every matrix is exactly symmetric.

functions.name: md1_scatter
functions.what: Write a `md1_pair` block into `M` at both `(sa, sb)` and `(sb, sa)`.

functions.name: md1_pick
functions.what: One matrix out of `md1_all`.

functions.name: md1_s
functions.what: Integral-stage members `(atoms, shells, prims) -> [n, n]`.

functions.name: md1_h
functions.what: The core Hamiltonian `T + V`.

functions.name: md1_gap
functions.what: Test helper: the largest absolute gap between matrix `k` of `M` and `R`.

functions.name: es_pair
functions.what: Index of the pair (i, j), in either order.

functions.name: es_npair
functions.what: Pairs of `n` orbitals.

functions.name: es_index8
functions.what: Packed-8 index of (ij|kl), for any of its eight index orders.

functions.name: es_len8
functions.what: Length of the packed-8 vector for `n` orbitals.

functions.name: es_get
functions.what: (ij|kl) read from the packed vector.

functions.name: es_pack8
functions.what: Pack a dense, 8-fold-symmetric `[n, n, n, n]` tensor. Only entries with i >= j, k >= l and ij >= kl are read.

functions.name: es_unpack8
functions.what: The dense `[n, n, n, n]` view of a packed vector. Meant for small `n`: the view holds $n^4$ doubles.

functions.name: es_rng
functions.what: One Park-Miller step on the state in `st[0]`; returns the new weight in $(0, 1)$. The state must start in `1 .. ES_MINSTD_M - 1`.

functions.name: es_checksums
functions.what: `[sum Gp^2, sum w_k Gp_k]`, summed in index order, with w_k the k-th Park-Miller weight from `seed`. The seeded sum catches errors that a sum of squares misses, such as two values swapped.

functions.name: es_sample_index
functions.what: `m` packed indices drawn with the same generator: floor(w_k * len). Indices can repeat.

functions.name: es_sample_gap
functions.what: The largest abs(Gp[idx[k]] - vals[k]) over the samples.

functions.name: es_sym_tensor
functions.what: Test helper: a dense tensor that is 8-fold symmetric bit for bit. Addition and multiplication of two doubles commute exactly, so building every entry from commutative pieces of (i, j) and of (k, l) makes all eight orders equal without relying on the packing code under test.

functions.name: es_sym_defect
functions.what: Test helper: the largest disagreement among the eight orders of any entry.

functions.name: mderi_packsize
functions.what: Entries of one pack for groups of `ca` and `cb` shells of angular momentum `la` and `lb` with `npp` primitive pairs: a 5-number header `[la, lb, npp, nab, nh]`, `(p, Px, Py, Pz)` per primitive pair, then `E_ab` as `[nab, npp * nh]`, `nab = ca cb ncart(la) ncart(lb)` rows.

functions.name: mderi_fillpack
functions.what: Fill the pack for the group pair of `nga` shells from `sa` and `ngb` from `sb` at `ST[off ..]`. `cn` is from `bas_contract`. The shells of a group share their primitives' exponents, so the primitive pairs, their centers and the Hermite expansions are the first shells'; each row of `E_ab` carries one shell pair's contraction coefficients, rows ordered `((a nb_grp + b) ncart_a + i) ncart_b + j` for shell `a` of the first group, `b` of the second, components `i` and `j`.

functions.name: mderi_store_groups
functions.what: The store for the group pairs in `PL` (`[npl, 2]`, rows `(ga, gb)`) of the groups `GT` (`[ng, 2]`, rows `(first shell, shells)`), as one flat array: `ST[0]` = pair count, `ST[1]` = largest l, then the directory (`MDERI_DIR_LEN` entries a pair), then the packs.

functions.name: mderi_store_pairs
functions.what: The store for the shell pairs in `PL` (`[npl, 2]`, rows `(sa, sb)`), each shell a group of its own.

functions.name: mderi_seg_groups
functions.what: Every shell a group of its own, `[nsh, 2]`: the segmented store.

functions.name: mderi_same_prims
functions.what: `1` when shells `s` and `t` are on the same atom, have the same angular momentum and the same primitive exponents: the contractions of one general contraction, which the basis tables list as segmented shells one after the other.

functions.name: mderi_groups
functions.what: The shell groups, `[ng, 2]` rows `(first shell, shells)`: runs of consecutive shells with the same atom, angular momentum and exponents. A group's primitive integrals are computed once for all its shells.

functions.name: mderi_canon_pairs
functions.what: Every canonical pair `a >= b` of `nsh` shells (or groups), numbered `a (a + 1)/2 + b`.

functions.name: mderi_store
functions.what: The store over every canonical pair of shell groups (`mderi_groups`): the production one.

functions.name: mderi_store_seg
functions.what: The store over every canonical shell pair, each shell its own group: the segmented store, which checks the grouped one.

functions.name: mderi_grid
functions.what: The Boys grid an ERI build needs: orders up to `4 lmax`.

functions.name: mderi_emat
functions.what: `E_ab` of the pack at `o`, copied out as a matrix for `@`.

functions.name: mderi_hoff
functions.what: Offsets `(t D + u) D + v` into an R cube of side `D`, for the Hermite list of order `L`; with `signed = 1`, the sign `(-1)^(t+u+v)` instead.

functions.name: mderi_block
functions.what: The block `(ab|cd)` for bra pair `k1` and ket pair `k2` of the store, as `[ncart_a * ncart_b, ncart_c * ncart_d]`. `G` is from `mderi_grid`.

functions.name: mderi_schwarz
functions.what: `Q[k] = sqrt(max (ab|ab))` over the components of store pair `k`.

functions.name: mderi_qlist
functions.what: The flat quartet list `[nq, 2]` of `(bra pair, ket pair)` rows with `bra >= ket`, keeping a row when `Q[bra] Q[ket] >= tol`. A negative `tol` keeps every row, and `Q` is then not read.

functions.name: mderi_put
functions.what: Write block `B` of store pairs `(k1, k2)` into the packed vector. Only the canonical entries (`i >= j`, `k >= l`, and `ij >= kl` when the two pairs are the same) are written, so every slot is written once.

functions.name: mderi_put_at
functions.what: `mderi_put` with the functions numbered by the shells-table columns `c0col` (first function) and `ncol` (how many): `SH_CART0` and `SH_NCART` for a Cartesian block, `SH_SPH0` and `SH_NSPH` for a spherical one. The shells are in the same order in both numberings, so the same canonical quartets hold every canonical integral of either. A row of the block is `((a nb_grp + b) n_a + i) n_b + j` (lib/hf/md_eri's pack rows), and within one group pair only `i >= j` (by function number) is written.

functions.name: mderi_do
functions.what: One row of the quartet list, computed and written; a def of its own so that its arrays are freed on return, on whichever thread ran it.

functions.name: mderi_build
functions.what: Packed-8 ERIs over Cartesian AOs, skipping quartets with `Q_AB Q_CD < tol` (a negative `tol` skips nothing and never computes `Q`), over the grouped store.

functions.name: mderi_build_st
functions.what: `mderi_build` over a given store: grouped or segmented.

functions.name: mderi_screened
functions.what: Integral-stage members `(atoms, shells, prims) -> packed-8`.

functions.name: mderi_tstore
functions.what: The pair transforms of the store's group pairs as one flat array. `TS[k]` is where pair k's matrix starts, `[rows of its block, nsph_a nsph_b times the shell pairs]`, block diagonal with one `M_a (x) M_b` per shell pair, followed by its transpose; `TS[k]` is `-1` when both groups are up to p, whose block of `M` is the identity. `M` is the c2s matrix of lib/hf/cart2sph.

functions.name: mderi_tmat
functions.what: The `[rows, cols]` matrix stored at `TS[o ..]`, copied out for `@`.

functions.name: mderi_block_sph
functions.what: The block `(ab|cd)` of store pairs `k1`, `k2` over spherical functions: the Cartesian block of `mderi_block` with the bra pair's transform transposed on the left and the ket pair's on the right (`mderi_tstore`), a side skipped when its transform is the identity.

functions.name: mderi_sph_do
functions.what: One row of the quartet list over spherical functions, computed, transformed and written; a def of its own so its arrays are freed on return.

functions.name: mderi_sph_build
functions.what: Packed-8 ERIs over spherical functions, `M` the c2s matrix: each quartet moved to spherical functions as it is computed, so no Cartesian packed vector is built and none is read back. Schwarz screening as in `mderi_build` (a negative `tol` skips nothing).

functions.name: mderi_sph
functions.what: The production ERIs over spherical functions: Schwarz-screened at `MDERI_SCREEN_TOL`, transformed block by block. `mderi_screened` followed by `tr4_blocks` (lib/hf/transform) is the same thing in two passes and checks it.

functions.name: mderi_quartet
functions.what: `(ab|cd)` for four shells in any order, `[na nb, nc nd]`: the entry point for single quartets and for tests.

functions.name: mderi_prim1_size
functions.what: Scratch entries `mderi_prim1` needs for components up to `lmax`.

functions.name: mderi_erow
functions.what: Where `E(la, lb, 0)` sits in a table `herm_efill` wrote at `e0` for powers `la`, `lb`.

functions.name: mderi_prim1
functions.what: One integral `(ab|cd)` over four unit-normalized primitive components. `PQ` is `[4, 7]`, a row `(exponent, x, y, z, lx, ly, lz)` per function; `G` is from `herm_grid` with order at least the total `l`; `W` is scratch of `mderi_prim1_size(lmax)` entries and `F` of `4 lmax + 1`. It builds only the E entries of these powers and only the R entries inside their box (`herm_rfill_box`), so one value costs far less than the shell block that holds it. It is the path for spot checks on bases too big for a full build, and it shares no matrix code with `mderi_block`.

functions.name: mderi_schwarz_excess
functions.what: Test helper: the largest `|(ij|kl)| / sqrt((ij|ij)(kl|kl)) - 1` over every packed entry; the Schwarz bound holds when it is at most rounding.

functions.name: mderi_diag_gap
functions.what: Test helper: the largest gap between the pair diagonal `(ij|ij)` of `Gp` and a reference list of it.

functions.name: mderi_ref_gaps
functions.what: Test helper: the largest of the relative checksum gaps and the sample and diagonal gaps of `Gp` against one reference set.

functions.name: scf_defaults
functions.what: The production options: every registry at its production member, DIIS over `OPT_DIIS_N_DEFAULT` matrices from the second iteration on (the guess's Fock matrix stays out, as in PySCF), at most `OPT_MAXIT_DEFAULT` iterations, converged at an energy change below `OPT_ETOL_DEFAULT` and a commutator below `OPT_GTOL_DEFAULT`, each integral stage by its production member.

functions.name: scf_checked
functions.what: The defaults with every integral stage cross-checked: all members run and must agree.

functions.name: opt_array
functions.what: The column array of options `o` for `na` alpha and `nb` beta electrons and nuclear repulsion `enuc`. `OPT_PRODUCTION` is `1` when `o.cross_check` is `0`.

functions.name: opt_new
functions.what: The column array of the defaults, with no electrons: what a registry member's own tests pass it.

functions.name: mdjk_put
functions.what: Add block `B` of store pairs `(k1, k2)` into the J and K copies of one chunk, `W[w0 + 2d]` (J) and `W[w0 + 2d + 1]` (K) for each density `d`. Rows and columns of `B` are numbered as lib/hf/md_eri's packs number them, a shell pair of the two groups at a time.

functions.name: mdjk_one
functions.what: One quartet of the list into chunk `c`'s copies; a def of its own so the block is freed as soon as it has been added.

functions.name: mdjk_chunk
functions.what: Chunk `c` of `nch`: quartets `c, c + nch, c + 2 nch, ...` of the list, added into `W`, the chunk's own copies of J and K.

functions.name: mdjk_direct_nch
functions.what: J and K with the quartets dealt into `nch` chunks. The result does not depend on the thread count; it depends on `nch` only through the order of the final sums.

functions.name: mdjk_direct
functions.what: The J/K registry member: `X1 .. X3` = atoms, shells, prims; `D` is `[ndens, n, n]`; the result is `[2 ndens, n, n]`, J then K per density.

functions.name: mdjk_dmax
functions.what: The largest `|D|` over the functions of each pair of shell groups (`GT`, lib/hf/md_eri's `mderi_groups`) and every density, `[ng, ng]`, symmetric. A group's functions are consecutive.

functions.name: mdjk_pair
functions.what: One quartet computed and added into `W`; a def of its own so the block is freed as soon as it has been added.

functions.name: mdjk_chunk_screened
functions.what: Chunk `c` of `nch` of the screened build: bra pairs `c, c + nch, ...`, each against every ket pair up to it, a quartet kept when it passes the Schwarz test (`Q_AB Q_CD >= tol_s`) and the density test (header), with `Dm` over the store's shell groups.

functions.name: mdjk_screened_q
functions.what: J and K of `D` with Schwarz and density screening, from the Schwarz factors `Q` of the store's pairs (`mderi_schwarz`); `[2 ndens, n, n]`.

functions.name: mdjk_direct_screened
functions.what: The density-screened J/K registry member: `X1 .. X3` = atoms, shells, prims. It computes the Schwarz factors itself; the SCF's direct member (lib/hf/jk_direct) takes them from the basis blob instead.

functions.name: mdjk_rand_dens
functions.what: Test helper: `nd` seeded symmetric densities `[nd, n, n]` with entries in (-1, 1), from the Park-Miller generator of `lib/hf/eri_store`.

functions.name: mdjk_dense_gap
functions.what: Test helper: J and K of `D` by dense contraction of the packed vector, as two `[n^2, n^2]` matrix-vector products: `J = Gj @ vec(D)` with `Gj[(i,j),(k,l)] = (ij|kl)`, and `K = Gk @ vec(D)` with `Gk[(i,j),(k,l)] = (ik|jl)`. The largest gap to `JK` over every entry is returned.

functions.what: One primitive pair of a `(3, 2)` shell pair, exponents `a` and `b`, centers `A - B = (X, Y, Z)`: `V[(i nb + j) nh + h] = N_i N_j E^x E^y E^z` for component `i` of the first shell, `j` of the second and Hermite function `h` of order `5`. Entries no component pair reaches are left as they are (the caller zeroes `V`). `EX`, `EY` and `EZ` are scratch for the E tables, `herm_esize(la, lb)` each.

functions.name: mdg_e_33
functions.what: The E table of one axis for powers up to `(3, 3)`, exponents `a` and `b`, `X = A - B` on the axis: `herm_efill(E, 0, la, lb, a, b, X)` without the loops.

functions.name: mdg_pair_33
functions.what: One primitive pair of a `(3, 3)` shell pair, exponents `a` and `b`, centers `A - B = (X, Y, Z)`: `V[(i nb + j) nh + h] = N_i N_j E^x E^y E^z` for component `i` of the first shell, `j` of the second and Hermite function `h` of order `6`. Entries no component pair reaches are left as they are (the caller zeroes `V`). `EX`, `EY` and `EZ` are scratch for the E tables, `herm_esize(la, lb)` each.

functions.name: mdg_gather_0
functions.what: The Hermite values of one primitive quartet with a ket pair of total order `0`, signed and gathered for the ket contraction: for each bra Hermite function `ha = (ta, ua, va)` of order up to `L1` and each ket one `h = (t, u, v)`, `BR[o + h ncol + ha] = (-1)^(t+u+v) R(ta + t, ua + u, va + v)`, `R` the cube of side `D` in `S` (`herm_rfill`'s layout). The ket offsets are constants; the bra ones are Int arithmetic, where mdg_eri's general gather reads both from a table.

functions.what: The Hermite values of one primitive quartet with a ket pair of total order `5`, signed and gathered for the ket contraction: for each bra Hermite function `ha = (ta, ua, va)` of order up to `L1` and each ket one `h = (t, u, v)`, `BR[o + h ncol + ha] = (-1)^(t+u+v) R(ta + t, ua + u, va + v)`, `R` the cube of side `D` in `S` (`herm_rfill`'s layout).
