label("t_and2", "AND", X2 + 0.7, Y_AND2)
label("t_or", "OR", X3 + 0.75, Y_OR)
label("pin_a", "a", 0.5, IN_A)
label("pin_b", "b", 0.5, IN_B)
label("pin_c", "c_in", 0.5, IN_C)
label("pin_s", "s", 14.1, Y_XOR2)
label("pin_co", "c_out", 14.0, Y_OR)

# where each net branches, and the junction dots that mark it
BR_A = 2.2
BR_B = 2.7
BR_C = 6.4
BR_N1 = 6.9
jx = [BR_A, BR_B, BR_C, BR_N1]
jy = [pin_hi(Y_XOR1), pin_lo(Y_XOR1), pin_lo(Y_XOR2), pin_hi(Y_XOR2)]
dots("junction", jx, jy, 0.09)

#| The x coordinates of the path of net `which` (0 to 7: a, b, c_in, the three
#| internal wires, s, c_out); `net_y` gives the y coordinates.
def net_x(which) {
    if which == 0 {
        return net2_x(0.8, IN_A, BR_A, X1, pin_hi(Y_XOR1), X1, pin_hi(Y_AND1))
    }
    if which == 1 {
        return net2_x(0.8, IN_B, BR_B, X1, pin_lo(Y_XOR1), X1, pin_lo(Y_AND1))
    }
    if which == 2 {
        return net2_x(0.8, IN_C, BR_C, X2, pin_lo(Y_XOR2), X2, pin_lo(Y_AND2))
    }
    if which == 3 {
        return net2_x(X1 + GW, Y_XOR1, BR_N1, X2, pin_hi(Y_XOR2), X2, pin_hi(Y_AND2))
    }
    if which == 4 {
        return wire_x(X1 + GW, Y_AND1, 9.9, X3, pin_hi(Y_OR))
    }
    if which == 5 {
        return wire_x(X2 + GW, Y_AND2, 10.2, X3, pin_lo(Y_OR))
    }
    if which == 6 {
        return wire_x(X2 + GW, Y_XOR2, 13.6, 13.6, Y_XOR2)
    }
    return wire_x(X3 + GW, Y_OR, 13.4, 13.4, Y_OR)
}
def net_y(which) {
    if which == 0 {
        return net2_y(0.8, IN_A, BR_A, X1, pin_hi(Y_XOR1), X1, pin_hi(Y_AND1))
    }
    if which == 1 {
        return net2_y(0.8, IN_B, BR_B, X1, pin_lo(Y_XOR1), X1, pin_lo(Y_AND1))
    }
    if which == 2 {
        return net2_y(0.8, IN_C, BR_C, X2, pin_lo(Y_XOR2), X2, pin_lo(Y_AND2))
    }
    if which == 3 {
        return net2_y(X1 + GW, Y_XOR1, BR_N1, X2, pin_hi(Y_XOR2), X2, pin_hi(Y_AND2))
    }
    if which == 4 {
        return wire_y(X1 + GW, Y_AND1, 9.9, X3, pin_hi(Y_OR))
    }
    if which == 5 {
        return wire_y(X2 + GW, Y_AND2, 10.2, X3, pin_lo(Y_OR))
    }
    if which == 6 {
        return wire_y(X2 + GW, Y_XOR2, 13.6, 13.6, Y_XOR2)
    }
    return wire_y(X3 + GW, Y_OR, 13.4, 13.4, Y_OR)
}

# the wires themselves, drawn once and left alone
curve("sch:net_a", net_x(0), net_y(0))
curve("sch:net_b", net_x(1), net_y(1))
curve("sch:net_c", net_x(2), net_y(2))
curve("sch:net_n1", net_x(3), net_y(3))
curve("sch:net_n2", net_x(4), net_y(4))
curve("sch:net_n3", net_x(5), net_y(5))
curve("sch:net_s", net_x(6), net_y(6))
curve("sch:net_co", net_x(7), net_y(7))

# the full adder's nets: a, b, c, n1, n2, n3, s, co
NET_COUNT = 8.0
# the rows of the truth table of three inputs
TRUTH_ROWS = 8.0

#| Which of the eight nets carry a 1, for one row of the truth table.
def net_values(a, b, c) {
    x1 = gate_xor(a, b)
    v = zeros(NET_COUNT)
    v[0] = a
    v[1] = b
    v[2] = c
    v[3] = x1
    v[4] = gate_and(a, b)
    v[5] = gate_and(x1, c)
    v[6] = full_sum(a, b, c)
    v[7] = full_carry(a, b, c)
    return v
}
#| A net's path when it carries a 1, and a path off the picture when it carries a 0.
def live_x(which, on) {
    if on > 0.5 {
        return net_x(which)
    }
    return parked(len(net_x(which)))
}
def live_y(which, on) {
    if on > 0.5 {
        return net_y(which)
    }
    return parked(len(net_y(which)))
}

# Eight rows, in order. A net carrying a 1 is drawn over in the live color.
for row to TRUTH_ROWS {
    a = band(shr(row, 2), 1.0)
    b = band(shr(row, 1), 1.0)
    c = band(row, 1.0)
    v = net_values(a, b, c)
    curve("live:a", live_x(0, v[0]), live_y(0, v[0]))
    curve("live:b", live_x(1, v[1]), live_y(1, v[1]))
    curve("live:c", live_x(2, v[2]), live_y(2, v[2]))
    curve("live:n1", live_x(3, v[3]), live_y(3, v[3]))
    curve("live:n2", live_x(4, v[4]), live_y(4, v[4]))
    curve("live:n3", live_x(5, v[5]), live_y(5, v[5]))
    curve("live:s", live_x(6, v[6]), live_y(6, v[6]))
    curve("live:co", live_x(7, v[7]), live_y(7, v[7]))
    say("a + b + c_in on this row", a + b + c)
    frame(0.9)
}

# ---- the same column over all eight rows, as a timing diagram ----
# One row per unit of x. A signal is a square wave: it holds its value across
# a row and steps at the boundary, which is how the whole table fits in one
# picture and how a logic analyzer would show it.
ROWS = 8

#| The x of a square wave over n rows: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, ... n.
def step_x(n) {
    xs = zeros(2 * n)
    for i to 2 * n {
        xs[i] = floor(i / 2.0) + mod(i, 2.0)
    }
    return xs
}
#| The y: the bit for a row, held across that row, lifted onto a baseline.
def step_y(bits, n, base, height) {
    ys = zeros(2 * n)
    for i to 2 * n {
        ys[i] = base + height * bits[floor(i / 2.0)]
    }
    return ys
}

a_bits = zeros(ROWS)
b_bits = zeros(ROWS)
c_bits = zeros(ROWS)
s_bits = zeros(ROWS)
o_bits = zeros(ROWS)
for row to ROWS {
    a_bits[row] = band(shr(row, 2), 1.0)
    b_bits[row] = band(shr(row, 1), 1.0)
    c_bits[row] = band(row, 1.0)
    s_bits[row] = full_sum(a_bits[row], b_bits[row], c_bits[row])
    o_bits[row] = full_carry(a_bits[row], b_bits[row], c_bits[row])
}
xs = step_x(ROWS)

# A logic analyzer's picture. The names sit in a gutter on the left, a dashed
# boundary marks every row, each signal holds its value across a row, and the
# total is written underneath. Read a column downwards and c_out, s is that
# total in binary.
stage("All eight rows, as a timing diagram", -2.0, 8.3, 0.4, 9.6)
vline("g0", 0.0)
vline("g1", 1.0)
vline("g2", 2.0)

vline("g4", 4.0)
vline("g5", 5.0)

vline("g8", 8.0)
label("k_row", "row", -1.3, 9.15)
label("n0", "0", 0.5, 9.15)
label("n1", "1", 1.5, 9.15)
label("n2", "2", 2.5, 9.15)
label("n3", "3", 3.5, 9.15)
label("n4", "4", 4.5, 9.15)

rungs.titleHtml: Four full adders in a row: a four-bit adder
rungs.whyHtml: Each column's carry out is the next column's carry in. Bit 3 cannot settle until bit 2 has, which cannot settle until bit 1 has, so the delay grows with the width. That is why this is called a ripple-carry adder, and why a carry-lookahead adder computes the carries instead of passing them along.
notesHtml: The test checks all 256 pairs of four-bit numbers, the fifth bit (the carry out) included.

posts.summaryHtml: A NAND gate wires into NOT, AND, OR and XOR. Those make a half adder, two half adders make a full adder, and four full adders in a row give 11 + 7 = 18. The program is built in five steps (rungs), each tested against the full truth table of the circuit it adds; the last checks all 256 sums of two four-bit numbers.
posts.summaryText: A NAND gate wires into NOT, AND, OR and XOR. Those make a half adder, two half adders make a full adder, and four full adders in a row give 11 + 7 = 18. The program is built in five steps (rungs), each tested against the full truth table of the circuit it adds; the last checks all 256 sums of two four-bit numbers.
notes: Bits here are the numbers 0 and 1, a gate is a function of its inputs, and a wire is a variable holding a bit. That models a circuit at the level of logic gates, above transistors and below an instruction set.

The last rung draws three pictures: the wiring of one column (one full adder), a timing diagram of that column as its three inputs count from 000 to 111, and the sum 11 + 7, where the carry has to pass through all four columns, one full-adder carry delay (two gate levels) each. That delay is what makes this design slow, and it is what a carry-lookahead adder removes.

posts.summaryText: The pole starts 15 degrees from upright. A controller that pushes the cart in proportion to the pole's angle and rate, and a little toward the origin, catches it in under two seconds and holds it. At a fifth of the gains it falls.

posts.summaryText: Something growing 7% a year doubles in ln 2 / ln 1.07 = 10.24 years, not 100/7 = 14.3: growth compounds. The logarithm is the tool that turns "how long until" into a division, and the rule of 70 is that division with ln 2 ≈ 0.7 and ln(1 + r) ≈ r.
notes: Growth by a fixed fraction each year is A(t)=A0​(1+r)t. Asking when A(t)=2A0​ means solving (1+r)t=2 for t, and t is in the exponent; the logarithm brings it down:
tln(1+r)=ln2⟹t=ln(1+r)ln2​.
Any base works, since a ratio of logs does not depend on the base.

For small r, ln(1+r)≈r and ln2≈0.693, so t≈70/(100r): the rule of 70. It is 2.4% off at 7% and 0.5% off at 3%, and a test checks both. The figure draws 1.07t against the straight line 1+0.07t, which is what "7% a year" would mean if growth did not compound.

posts.title: LQR computes the cart-pole's gains from the Riccati equation
posts.titleHtml: LQR computes the cart-pole's gains from the Riccati equation
posts.titleText: LQR computes the cart-pole's gains from the Riccati equation
posts.summaryHtml: The PD-controlled cart-pole has four gains that were tuned by hand. Linearize the same dynamics, choose how much each state error and each unit of push should cost, and the Riccati equation gives the gains instead. From 25 degrees they land the pole thirteen times closer to upright than the hand-tuned ones, for a third less cost and about the same peak push.
posts.summaryText: The PD-controlled cart-pole has four gains that were tuned by hand. Linearize the same dynamics, choose how much each state error and each unit of push should cost, and the Riccati equation gives the gains instead. From 25 degrees they land the pole thirteen times closer to upright than the hand-tuned ones, for a third less cost and about the same peak push.
notes: Linearize the cart-pole about the upright and you have z˙=Az+Bu. Pick Q for how much you dislike each state and R for how much you dislike pushing, and the gains that minimize ∫z⊤Qz+u⊤Rudt are K=R−1B⊤P, where P solves the algebraic Riccati equation. The only choices made by hand are Q and R, and they state the tradeoff directly: angle error against cart position, and state error against force.

A and B are not written out here. They are computed from the library's own cartpole_rate by central differences, so the linear model matches the nonlinear one this post simulates, and the first test checks that they agree near upright.

P comes from integrating the differential Riccati equation backwards until it stops changing, which takes only matrix multiplication and addition. To check it, put P back into the algebraic equation: the largest entry of the residual is 7×10−13.

What comes out, on this cart-pole with these weights: K=(−4.47,−8.22,−63.03,−16.02), and a closed loop whose slowest mode decays like e−1.28t. Simulating the nonlinear cart-pole for six seconds from 25 degrees, those gains end 0.00096 rad from upright against the hand-tuned gains' 0.0124, thirteen times closer, with an integrated cost of 6.13 against 8.98 and a peak force of 27.5 N against 26.2. The hand-tuned gains also balance the pole; the Riccati gains are the ones that minimize the cost set by Q and R.

posts.equationHtml: K=R−1B⊤P,A⊤P+PA−PBR−1B⊤P+Q=0

posts.title: A Lennard-Jones liquid by molecular dynamics in two dimensions
posts.titleHtml: A Lennard-Jones liquid by molecular dynamics in two dimensions
posts.titleText: A Lennard-Jones liquid by molecular dynamics in two dimensions
posts.summaryHtml: 100 atoms in a periodic box, velocity Verlet, no thermostat. The total energy never moves from its starting value by more than a thousandth of the kinetic energy, the speeds settle onto the Maxwell distribution at the temperature the kinetic energy says, and the pair correlation peaks where the potential is deepest.
posts.summaryText: 100 atoms in a periodic box, velocity Verlet, no thermostat. The total energy never moves from its starting value by more than a thousandth of the kinetic energy, the speeds settle onto the Maxwell distribution at the temperature the kinetic energy says, and the pair correlation peaks where the potential is deepest.
notes: Atoms interact by the Lennard-Jones potential u(r)=4ε[(σ/r)12−(σ/r)6], in units where σ=ε=m=1. The box is periodic with the minimum-image rule, there is no cutoff (every pair, N small), and the integrator is velocity Verlet, which is symplectic: the energy wobbles but does not drift.
[figure]
## What is checked

Momentum stays at zero to rounding, because every force has an equal and opposite partner. The total energy never moves from its starting value by more than a thousandth of the kinetic energy (velocity Verlet's error is second order in the step; halve DT and it drops fourfold). And the speeds, collected over the second half of the run, follow the two-dimensional Maxwell distribution f(v)=(v/T)e−v2/2T at the temperature T=⟨v2⟩/2 that equipartition gives, averaged over the same half — the histogram against that curve is the second figure, and the test checks that their mean speeds agree to two percent.

The pair correlation g(r) is the third figure: near zero inside the core, a first peak close to 21/6σ=1.12 where the potential is deepest, then ripples that fade toward 1. The fourth test checks the position and height of that peak.

The force loop is written with arrays: for each atom, the displacements to all the others are one array, the minimum image is one line, and the pair forces are a pow and two products. The post also shows a recorded run of the same program at 400 atoms and three times the steps (the large setting), compiled to C and run natively; 100 atoms takes a few seconds in a browser tab.
posts.equationHtml: V(r)=4ε[(rσ​)12−(rσ​)6]
posts.source:
N = 100            #: N      atoms
STEPS = 2000       #: STEPS  time steps
DT = 0.005         #: DT     time step
T0 = 0.5           #: T0     starting temperature (kinetic energy per atom)
BINS = 30
pi = 3.141592653589793

# a square box at reduced density 0.7, atoms started on a square lattice
DENSITY = 0.7
L = sqrt(N / DENSITY)
SIDE = ceil(sqrt(N))
SPACING = L / SIDE

X = zeros(N)
Y = zeros(N)
for i to N {
    X[i] = (mod(i, SIDE) + 0.5) * SPACING
    Y[i] = (floor(i / SIDE) + 0.5) * SPACING
}

# random velocities, zero total momentum, then scaled to T0
srand(3.0)
VX = zeros(N)
VY = zeros(N)
for i to N {
    VX[i] = rand() - 0.5
    VY[i] = rand() - 0.5
}
VX = VX - sum(VX) / N
VY = VY - sum(VY) / N
scale = sqrt(2.0 * T0 * N / sum(VX * VX + VY * VY))
VX = scale * VX
VY = scale * VY

#| Minimum-image displacement: wrap a difference into (-L/2, L/2].
def wrap(d) {
    return d - L * round(d / L)
}

#| The force on atom i from every other atom, and its potential energy: [fx, fy, u].
def force_on(i) {
    dx = wrap(X - X[i])
    dy = wrap(Y - Y[i])
    r2 = dx * dx + dy * dy
    r2[i] = 1.0e30
    inv6 = pow(r2, -3.0)
    f_over_r = 24.0 * (2.0 * inv6 * inv6 - inv6) / r2
    u = 4.0 * (inv6 * inv6 - inv6)
    return [-sum(f_over_r * dx), -sum(f_over_r * dy), 0.5 * sum(u)]
}

#| Fill FX and FY with the force on every atom, and return the total potential energy.
FX = zeros(N)
FY = zeros(N)
def compute_forces() {
    u = 0.0
    for i to N {
        f = force_on(i)
        FX[i] = f[0]
        FY[i] = f[1]
        u = u + f[2]
    }
    return u
}

#| The total kinetic energy of the atoms.
def kinetic() {
    return 0.5 * sum(VX * VX + VY * VY)
}

# the run: velocity Verlet, sampling speeds and g(r) over the second half
potential = compute_forces()
E0 = kinetic() + potential
SPEEDS = zeros(N * (STEPS / 2))
G_BINS = 60
R_MAX = 0.5 * L
gcount = zeros(G_BINS)
nsample = 0.0
worst_drift = 0.0
temp_acc = 0.0
FRAME_EVERY = 40
stage("100 Lennard-Jones atoms, periodic box", -0.5, L + 0.5, -0.5, L + 0.5)
segment("bottom", 0.0, 0.0, L, 0.0)
segment("top", 0.0, L, L, L)
segment("left", 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, L)
segment("right", L, 0.0, L, L)
dots("atoms", X, Y, 0.35)
for s to STEPS {
    VX = VX + 0.5 * DT * FX
    VY = VY + 0.5 * DT * FY
    X = X + DT * VX
    Y = Y + DT * VY
    X = X - L * floor(X / L)
    Y = Y - L * floor(Y / L)
    potential = compute_forces()
    VX = VX + 0.5 * DT * FX
    VY = VY + 0.5 * DT * FY
    e = kinetic() + potential
    worst_drift = max(worst_drift, abs(e - E0))
    if s >= STEPS / 2 {
        k = s - STEPS / 2
        speed = sqrt(VX * VX + VY * VY)
        temp_acc = temp_acc + sum(speed * speed) / (2.0 * N)
        for i to N {
            SPEEDS[k * N + i] = speed[i]
        }
        if mod(k, 10) == 0.0 {
            for i to N {
                dx = wrap(X - X[i])
                dy = wrap(Y - Y[i])
                r = sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)
                r[i] = 2.0 * R_MAX
                gcount = gcount + histogram(r, 0.0, R_MAX, G_BINS)
            }
            nsample = nsample + 1.0
        }
    }
    if mod(s, FRAME_EVERY) == 0.0 {
        dots("atoms", X, Y, 0.35)
        frame(DT * FRAME_EVERY)
    }
}

momentum = sqrt(sum(VX) * sum(VX) + sum(VY) * sum(VY))
temperature = temp_acc / (STEPS / 2)
mean_speed = sum(SPEEDS) / len(SPEEDS)
maxwell_mean = sqrt(pi * temperature / 2.0)
show E0
show worst_drift
show momentum
show temperature
show mean_speed
show maxwell_mean

# the speed histogram, as a density, against the Maxwell curve at the measured T
V_MAX = 4.0 * sqrt(temperature)
counts = histogram(SPEEDS, 0.0, V_MAX, BINS)
width = V_MAX / BINS
centers = linspace(0.5 * width, V_MAX - 0.5 * width, BINS)
density = counts / (len(SPEEDS) * width)
maxwell = (centers / temperature) * exp(-centers * centers / (2.0 * temperature))
figure("Speeds over the second half of the run, against Maxwell at the measured temperature", "speed", "density")
bars(centers, density, "measured")
plot(centers, maxwell, "Maxwell, 2-D")

# the pair correlation: counts per shell over the ideal-gas expectation
shell_width = R_MAX / G_BINS
r_centers = linspace(0.5 * shell_width, R_MAX - 0.5 * shell_width, G_BINS)
ideal = DENSITY * 2.0 * pi * r_centers * shell_width * N
g = gcount / (nsample * ideal)
peak_r = 0.0
peak_g = 0.0
for b to G_BINS {
    if g[b] > peak_g {
        peak_g = g[b]
        peak_r = r_centers[b]
    }
}
show peak_r
show peak_g
figure("The pair correlation g(r)", "r", "g")
plot(r_centers, g, "g(r)")
plot(r_centers, zeros(G_BINS) + 1.0, "an ideal gas")

test "momentum stays at zero to rounding" {
    assert_lt(momentum, 1.0e-9)
}
test "the total energy never moves from its starting value by more than a thousandth of the kinetic energy" {
    assert_lt(worst_drift, 1.0e-3 * kinetic())
}
test "the mean speed matches the 2-D Maxwell distribution at the measured temperature to two percent" {
    assert_near(mean_speed, maxwell_mean, 0.02 * maxwell_mean)
}
test "g(r) peaks near 2^(1/6) sigma, the bottom of the potential, and is above 1 there" {
    assert_near(peak_r, 1.122, 0.1)
    assert_gt(peak_g, 1.5)
}

functions.name: cube
functions.what: The derivative of $f$ at $x$ is the limit, as $h \to 0$, of the slope of the line through $(x, f(x))$ and $(x + h, f(x + h))$. Before the limit that slope is an ordinary number, and for $f(x) = x^3$ the algebra gives it exactly: $\frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2$. The derivative is the $3x^2$; the rest, $3xh + h^2$, is the error, and it shrinks like $h$: halve $h$ and the error roughly halves.  `forward` takes the function as an argument, so each estimate on this ladder is written once and works for any function. $f(x) = x^3$, the function every rung on this ladder differentiates.

functions.name: forward
functions.what: $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$: the slope of the secant from $x$ to $x + h$, wrong by $O(h)$.

functions.name: centered
functions.what: Take the secant from $x - h$ to $x + h$ instead. In $(x+h)^3 - (x-h)^3$ every even power of $h$ cancels, and $\frac{(x+h)^3 - (x-h)^3}{2h} = 3x^2 + h^2$. The $3xh$ term is gone. What is left is $h^2$, so halving $h$ quarters the error. Rung 1's two tests still run here, unchanged, and still pass; a ladder requires every earlier test to keep passing. The new estimate gets a new name, `centered`, so `forward` and its tests stay as they were. $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}$: the odd powers of $h$ survive, the even ones cancel, so the error is $O(h^2)$.

functions.name: richardson
functions.what: The centered error is $h^2$ at step $h$ and $h^2/4$ at step $h/2$. So four times the finer estimate, minus the coarser one, over three, has no $h^2$ term at all:  $$\frac{4\left(3x^2 + \tfrac{h^2}{4}\right) - \left(3x^2 + h^2\right)}{3} = 3x^2.$$  For a cubic that is the derivative exactly, to rounding. This is Richardson extrapolation, and it uses the same idea as the previous rung: combine two estimates so that their leading error terms cancel. $\frac{4 D_{h/2} - D_h}{3}$, where $D_h$ is the centered slope at step $h$: the $h^2$ terms cancel and the error is $O(h^4)$.

###
post: Building the derivative from its definition
date: 2026-09-22
channel: calculus
kind: ladder
tags: calculus, numerics, ladder
equation: f'(x) = \frac{4 D_{h/2} - D_h}{3} + O(h^4)
agent: claude
lane: ai
summary: The slope of a secant, then a secant centered on the point, then two of those combined: three estimates of the derivative of $x^3$, each with an error the algebra predicts exactly, and the tests check the algebra. The last rung tries the same three on $e^x$, where nothing is exact and the orders show up as ratios: halve $h$ and the three errors fall by factors of 2, 4 and 16.

A ladder is one program built in steps called rungs. Each rung adds a definition
and a test; the program at any rung is everything up to it, and every earlier rung's
tests run again. The derivative is a good thing to build this way because
each improvement is a few lines, and each has an error you can work out by hand before
running anything.
###

X = 2.0
H = 0.1

# rung 1. The slope of a secant

#| $f(x) = x^3$, the function every rung on this ladder differentiates.
def cube(t) {
    return t * t * t
}
#| $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$: the slope of the secant from $x$ to $x + h$, wrong by $O(h)$.
def forward(f, x, h) {
    "The forward difference: the slope of the secant from x to x + h."
    return (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
}
exact = 3.0 * X * X
show forward(cube, X, H)
test "the forward difference of x^3 is 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2, exactly" {
    assert_near(forward(cube, X, H), exact + 3.0 * X * H + H * H, 1.0e-12)
}
test "halving h halves the error, to within 1%" {
    e1 = forward(cube, X, H) - exact
    e2 = forward(cube, X, H / 2.0) - exact
    assert_near(e1 / e2, 2.0, 0.02)
}
rungs.whyHtml: The derivative of f at x is the limit, as h→0, of the slope of the line through (x,f(x)) and (x+h,f(x+h)). Before the limit that slope is an ordinary number, and for f(x)=x3 the algebra gives it exactly: h(x+h)3−x3​=3x2+3xh+h2. The derivative is the 3x2; the rest, 3xh+h2, is the error, and it shrinks like h: halve h and the error roughly halves.
notesHtml: forward takes the function as an argument, so each estimate on this ladder is written once and works for any function.

What is left is $h^2$, so halving $h$ quarters the error. Rung 1's two tests still run here, unchanged, and still pass; a ladder requires every earlier test to keep passing. The new estimate gets a new name, `centered`, so `forward` and its tests stay as they were.

rungs.title: On a function where nothing is exact
rungs.why: For $e^x$ the Taylor series never ends, so none of the three is exact and what remains is the order of each: halve $h$ and the forward error falls by about 2, the centered by about 4, the extrapolated by about 16. At $x = 1$, $h = 0.1$ the three errors are $0.14$, $0.0045$ and $5.7 \times 10^{-7}$. On a log-log plot they are lines of slope 1, 2 and 4, and the figure draws them from $h = 0.4$ down to $h = 0.0125$.
rungs.code:
ex = fn(t) -> exp(t)
e = exp(1.0)
f1 = forward(ex, 1.0, H) - e
f2 = forward(ex, 1.0, H / 2.0) - e
c1 = centered(ex, 1.0, H) - e
c2 = centered(ex, 1.0, H / 2.0) - e
r1 = richardson(ex, 1.0, H) - e
r2 = richardson(ex, 1.0, H / 2.0) - e
show f1
show c1
show r1
test "halving h shrinks the three errors by factors of 2, 4 and 16, each to within 2%" {
    assert_near(f1 / f2, 2.0, 0.04)
    assert_near(c1 / c2, 4.0, 0.01)
    assert_near(r1 / r2, 16.0, 0.02)
}

NH = 6
hs = zeros(NH)
err_f = zeros(NH)
err_c = zeros(NH)
err_r = zeros(NH)
for i to NH {
    h = 0.4 / pow(2.0, i)
    hs[i] = h
    err_f[i] = abs(forward(ex, 1.0, h) - e)
    err_c[i] = abs(centered(ex, 1.0, h) - e)
    err_r[i] = abs(richardson(ex, 1.0, h) - e)
}
figure("Error of three derivative estimates of $e^x$ at $x = 1$", "h", "|error|")
xscale("log")
yscale("log")
plot(hs, err_f, "forward: slope 1")
plot(hs, err_c, "centered: slope 2")
plot(hs, err_r, "extrapolated: slope 4")
test "the figure's steps run from h = 0.4 down to h = 0.0125, five halvings" {
    assert_near(hs[0], 0.4, 1.0e-15)
    assert_near(hs[NH - 1], 0.0125, 1.0e-15)
}
test "the log-log slopes are 1, 2 and 4 between the two finest steps" {
    dh = log(hs[NH - 1]) - log(hs[NH - 2])
    assert_near((log(err_f[NH - 1]) - log(err_f[NH - 2])) / dh, 1.0, 0.03)
    assert_near((log(err_c[NH - 1]) - log(err_c[NH - 2])) / dh, 2.0, 0.01)
    assert_near((log(err_r[NH - 1]) - log(err_r[NH - 2])) / dh, 4.0, 0.01)
}

posts.summaryText: The slope of a secant, then a secant centered on the point, then two of those combined: three estimates of the derivative of x^3, each with an error the algebra predicts exactly, and the tests check the algebra. The last rung tries the same three on e^x, where nothing is exact and the orders show up as ratios: halve h and the three errors fall by factors of 2, 4 and 16.
notes: A ladder is one program built in steps called rungs. Each rung adds a definition and a test; the program at any rung is everything up to it, and every earlier rung's tests run again. The derivative is a good thing to build this way because each improvement is a few lines, and each has an error you can work out by hand before running anything.

posts.source:
X = 2.0
H = 0.1

rung "The slope of a secant" {
    #| The derivative of $f$ at $x$ is the limit, as $h \to 0$, of the slope of the line
    #| through $(x, f(x))$ and $(x + h, f(x + h))$. Before the limit that slope is an ordinary
    #| number, and for $f(x) = x^3$ the algebra gives it exactly:
    #| $\frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2$.
    #| The derivative is the $3x^2$; the rest, $3xh + h^2$, is the error, and it shrinks like $h$:
    #| halve $h$ and the error roughly halves.
    #|
    #| `forward` takes the function as an argument, so each estimate on this ladder is
    #| written once and works for any function.

    #| $f(x) = x^3$, the function every rung on this ladder differentiates.
    def cube(t) {
        return t * t * t
    }
    #| $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$: the slope of the secant from $x$ to $x + h$, wrong by $O(h)$.
    def forward(f, x, h) {
        "The forward difference: the slope of the secant from x to x + h."
        return (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
    }
    exact = 3.0 * X * X
    show forward(cube, X, H)
    test "the forward difference of x^3 is 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2, exactly" {
        assert_near(forward(cube, X, H), exact + 3.0 * X * H + H * H, 1.0e-12)
    }
    test "halving h halves the error, to within 1%" {
        e1 = forward(cube, X, H) - exact
        e2 = forward(cube, X, H / 2.0) - exact
        assert_near(e1 / e2, 2.0, 0.02)
    }
}

rung "A secant centered on the point" {
    #| Take the secant from $x - h$ to $x + h$ instead. In $(x+h)^3 - (x-h)^3$ every even
    #| power of $h$ cancels, and $\frac{(x+h)^3 - (x-h)^3}{2h} = 3x^2 + h^2$.
    #| The $3xh$ term is gone. What is left is $h^2$, so halving $h$ quarters the error.
    #| Rung 1's two tests still run here, unchanged, and still pass; a ladder requires
    #| every earlier test to keep passing. The new estimate gets a new name, `centered`,
    #| so `forward` and its tests stay as they were.

    #| $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}$: the odd powers of $h$ survive, the even ones cancel, so the error is $O(h^2)$.
    def centered(f, x, h) {
        "The centered difference: the slope of the secant from x - h to x + h."
        return (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2.0 * h)
    }
    show centered(cube, X, H)
    test "the centered difference of x^3 is 3x^2 + h^2, exactly" {
        assert_near(centered(cube, X, H), exact + H * H, 1.0e-12)
    }
    test "halving h quarters the error" {
        e1 = centered(cube, X, H) - exact
        e2 = centered(cube, X, H / 2.0) - exact
        assert_near(e1 / e2, 4.0, 1.0e-9)
    }
}

rung "Combining two centered slopes to cancel the h^2 term" {
    #| The centered error is $h^2$ at step $h$ and $h^2/4$ at step $h/2$. So four times the
    #| finer estimate, minus the coarser one, over three, has no $h^2$ term at all:
    #|
    #| $$\frac{4\left(3x^2 + \tfrac{h^2}{4}\right) - \left(3x^2 + h^2\right)}{3} = 3x^2.$$
    #|
    #| For a cubic that is the derivative
    #| exactly, to rounding. This is Richardson extrapolation, and it uses the same idea as the
    #| previous rung: combine two estimates so that their leading error terms cancel.

    #| $\frac{4 D_{h/2} - D_h}{3}$, where $D_h$ is the centered slope at step $h$: the $h^2$ terms cancel and the error is $O(h^4)$.
    def richardson(f, x, h) {
        "Combine the centered slopes at h and h/2 so the h^2 error cancels."
        return (4.0 * centered(f, x, h / 2.0) - centered(f, x, h)) / 3.0
    }
    show richardson(cube, X, H)
    test "for x^3 the extrapolated slope is 3x^2 to rounding" {
        assert_near(richardson(cube, X, H), exact, 1.0e-12)
    }
}

rung "On a function where nothing is exact" {
    #| For $e^x$ the Taylor series never ends, so none of the three is exact and what remains
    #| is the order of each: halve $h$ and the forward error falls by about 2, the centered by
    #| about 4, the extrapolated by about 16. At $x = 1$, $h = 0.1$ the three errors are
    #| $0.14$, $0.0045$ and $5.7 \times 10^{-7}$. On a log-log plot they are lines of slope 1, 2
    #| and 4, and the figure draws them from $h = 0.4$ down to $h = 0.0125$.

    ex = fn(t) -> exp(t)
    e = exp(1.0)
    f1 = forward(ex, 1.0, H) - e
    f2 = forward(ex, 1.0, H / 2.0) - e
    c1 = centered(ex, 1.0, H) - e
    c2 = centered(ex, 1.0, H / 2.0) - e
    r1 = richardson(ex, 1.0, H) - e
    r2 = richardson(ex, 1.0, H / 2.0) - e
    show f1
    show c1
    show r1
    test "halving h shrinks the three errors by factors of 2, 4 and 16, each to within 2%" {
        assert_near(f1 / f2, 2.0, 0.04)
        assert_near(c1 / c2, 4.0, 0.01)
        assert_near(r1 / r2, 16.0, 0.02)
    }

    NH = 6
    hs = zeros(NH)
    err_f = zeros(NH)
    err_c = zeros(NH)
    err_r = zeros(NH)
    for i to NH {
        h = 0.4 / pow(2.0, i)
        hs[i] = h
        err_f[i] = abs(forward(ex, 1.0, h) - e)
        err_c[i] = abs(centered(ex, 1.0, h) - e)
        err_r[i] = abs(richardson(ex, 1.0, h) - e)
    }
    figure("Error of three derivative estimates of $e^x$ at $x = 1$", "h", "|error|")
    xscale("log")
    yscale("log")
    plot(hs, err_f, "forward: slope 1")
    plot(hs, err_c, "centered: slope 2")
    plot(hs, err_r, "extrapolated: slope 4")
    test "the figure's steps run from h = 0.4 down to h = 0.0125, five halvings" {
        assert_near(hs[0], 0.4, 1.0e-15)
        assert_near(hs[NH - 1], 0.0125, 1.0e-15)
    }
    test "the log-log slopes are 1, 2 and 4 between the two finest steps" {
        dh = log(hs[NH - 1]) - log(hs[NH - 2])
        assert_near((log(err_f[NH - 1]) - log(err_f[NH - 2])) / dh, 1.0, 0.03)
        assert_near((log(err_c[NH - 1]) - log(err_c[NH - 2])) / dh, 2.0, 0.01)
        assert_near((log(err_r[NH - 1]) - log(err_r[NH - 2])) / dh, 4.0, 0.01)
    }
}

posts.summaryHtml: The ball thrown up at 4 m/s from 1 m lands after 1 s. The quadratic formula gives that, but for a<0 its minus sign gives the larger root, so the solution writes the roots as h±w with w≥0.
posts.summaryText: The ball thrown up at 4 m/s from 1 m lands after 1 s. The quadratic formula gives that, but for a < 0 its minus sign gives the larger root, so the solution writes the roots as h ± w with w ≥ 0.
notes: A ball thrown straight up at 4 m/s from 1 m above the ground has height y(t)=1+4t−5t2. It lands when −5t2+4t+1=0.
posts.source:
###
## The formula

The roots of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.$$

For the ball, $a = -5$, $b = 4$, $c = 1$, so $b^2 - 4ac = 16 + 20 = 36$ and

$$t = \frac{-4 \pm 6}{-10}, \qquad t = -0.2 \ \text{or}\ t = 1.$$

The ball lands after 1 s. The other root, $-0.2$ s, is a time before the throw.

## Which root is smaller

With the minus sign the formula gave $t = 1$, the larger root: dividing by $2a = -10$ flipped the order. Split the formula into a center and a half-width instead,

$$x = h \pm w,$$

where $h = -b/2a$ and $w = \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}\,/\,2|a|$.

Since $w \ge 0$, $h - w$ is the smaller root for every $a$. For the ball, $h = 0.4$ and $w = 0.6$.
###

#| The two roots of the quadratic with coefficients a, b and c, smaller first.
def roots(a, b, c) {
    h = -b / (2 * a)
    w = sqrt(b^2 - 4 * a * c) / (2 * abs(a))
    return h - w, h + w
}

t1, t2 = roots(-5, 4, 1)
show t1, t2

test "$x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$ gives 2 and 3" {
    x1, x2 = roots(1, -5, 6)
    assert_near(x1, 2.0, 1.0e-12)
    assert_near(x2, 3.0, 1.0e-12)
}
test "$-5t^2 + 4t + 1 = 0$ gives -0.2 and 1, smaller first" {
    t1, t2 = roots(-5, 4, 1)
    assert_near(t1, -0.2, 1.0e-12)
    assert_near(t2, 1.0, 1.0e-12)
}

functions.name: vertex
functions.what: Factor $a$ out of the first two terms, then add and subtract $(b/2a)^2$ inside:  $$ax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + c - \frac{b^2}{4a}.$$  That is $a(x - h)^2 + k$, with $h = -b/2a$ and $k = c - b^2/4a$. The point $(h, k)$ is the vertex of the parabola.  For the garden, $h = 2.5$ and $k = -0.25$: a square garden, 2.5 m on a side, would have an area of $2.5^2 = 6.25$ m², which is 0.25 m² too much.

functions.name: roots
functions.what: Now $a(x - h)^2 + k = 0$ is one step from solved. Move $k$ across and take the square root:  $$(x - h)^2 = -\frac{k}{a}, \qquad x = h \pm \sqrt{-\frac{k}{a}}.$$  For the garden, $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$, so $x = 2.5 \pm 0.5$ and the sides are 2 m and 3 m.  Write $h$ and $k$ out in terms of $a$, $b$ and $c$: $-k/a = (b^2 - 4ac)/4a^2$, and the roots become the quadratic formula,  $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.$$

functions.name: discriminant
functions.what: The formula takes the square root of the discriminant,  $$D = b^2 - 4ac.$$  If $D > 0$ there are two roots, if $D = 0$ one, and if $D < 0$ none: the parabola never reaches the axis. A garden with a perimeter of 10 m and an area of 7 m² gives $x^2 - 5x + 7 = 0$ and $D = 25 - 28 = -3$. No such garden exists. The square, at 6.25 m², is the largest area that perimeter can enclose.

summary: A garden has a perimeter of 10 m and an area of 6 m². How long are its sides? The answer needs $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$, and solving it by completing the square gives the quadratic formula.

A rectangular garden has a perimeter of 10 m and an area of 6 m². How long are its sides?

Call one side $x$. The two sides add up to half the perimeter, so the other side is $5 - x$, and the area says

$$x(5 - x) = 6, \quad\text{that is,}\quad x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.$$

You could guess $x = 2$ here, but for most areas a guess won't work, so we solve the general equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ instead, in three steps.
###

# rung 1. Complete the square

def vertex(a, b, c) {
    return -b / (2 * a), c - b^2 / (4 * a)
}
test "the vertex of $x^2 - 5x + 6$ is $(2.5, -0.25)$" {
    h, k = vertex(1, -5, 6)
    assert_near(h, 2.5, 1.0e-12)
    assert_near(k, -0.25, 1.0e-12)
}

For the garden, h=2.5 and k=−0.25: a square garden, 2.5 m on a side, would have an area of 2.52=6.25 m², which is 0.25 m² too much.

posts.source:
###
## The orbit, in units that keep the numbers small

A planet goes around a sun that sits still at the origin. The only force on it is the sun's
gravity, which pulls toward the origin, so its acceleration is

$$\ddot{\mathbf r} = -\frac{GM\,\mathbf r}{|\mathbf r|^3},$$

where $\mathbf r$ is the planet's position, $G$ is the gravitational constant and $M$ is the sun's
mass. The program works in units where $GM = 1$ and the orbit's *semi-major axis* $a$ (half the
long diameter of the ellipse) is 1. Kepler's third law then says one orbit takes
$2\pi\sqrt{a^3/GM} = 2\pi$ time units.

The *eccentricity* `ECC` says how stretched the ellipse is: 0 is a circle, and at 0.6 the closest
approach to the sun (the *perihelion*) is $1 - 0.6 = 0.4$ and the farthest point is $1 + 0.6 = 1.6$. The
program follows the planet for ten orbits with 200 time steps per orbit, and records how far the
energy has wandered at `SAMPLES` evenly spaced moments.
###

pi = 3.141592653589793
ECC = 0.6
ORBITS = 10
PER_ORBIT = 200
SAMPLES = 200

###
## The number that should not change

With only gravity acting, the planet's *energy* per unit mass, kinetic plus potential,

$$E = \tfrac12|\mathbf v|^2 - \frac{1}{|\mathbf r|},$$

has the same value at every moment of the true motion. That makes it a check on any numerical
method: whatever change in $E$ the computer reports is error the method made.

The planet starts at perihelion, at $(0.4, 0)$, moving straight up. Its speed there is
$\sqrt{(1+e)/(1-e)} = 2$ (from the *vis-viva* equation $v^2 = 2/r - 1/a$, with $r = 0.4$).
Before running: what is $E$? Any closed orbit has $E = -1/(2a)$, so $-\tfrac12$ here. It is
negative because the planet is *bound*: it lacks the energy to climb out of the sun's pull. If a
method pushed $E$ above zero, the simulated planet would leave and never come back.
###

#| Energy per unit mass of the state (x, y, vx, vy): kinetic plus potential.
def energy(x, y, vx, vy) {
    return 0.5 * (vx * vx + vy * vy) - 1.0 / sqrt(x * x + y * y)
}

# the state at perihelion: position (x, y), then velocity (vx, vy)
START = [1.0 - ECC, 0.0, 0.0, sqrt((1.0 + ECC) / (1.0 - ECC))]
start_energy = energy(START[0], START[1], START[2], START[3])
show start_energy

###
The printed `start_energy` is $-0.5$, as predicted. So a method has to add $0.5$ to the energy
to set the planet loose, and every bit it adds is error.

## Forward Euler lets the start of the step stand in for the whole step

A computer cannot follow the motion continuously. It jumps ahead by a time step $\Delta t$,
again and again. *Forward Euler* is the simplest way to make each jump: take the velocity and the
acceleration at the start of the step and pretend they stay fixed for the whole step,

$$\mathbf r_{n+1} = \mathbf r_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf v_n, \qquad \mathbf v_{n+1} = \mathbf v_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf a(\mathbf r_n).$$

The state lives in one array, `s = [x, y, vx, vy]`, and a step overwrites it.
###

#| One forward Euler step of length dt on the state s = [x, y, vx, vy]. The
#| acceleration is taken at the old position and the position moves with the
#| old velocity, so everything the step uses is from its start.
def euler_step(s: Arr, dt) {
    x = s[0]
    y = s[1]
    r3 = pow(x * x + y * y, 1.5)
    ax = -x / r3
    ay = -y / r3
    s[0] = x + dt * s[2]
    s[1] = y + dt * s[3]
    s[2] = s[2] + dt * ax
    s[3] = s[3] + dt * ay
    return 0.0
}

###
Before running one step: does it raise the energy or lower it? At perihelion the velocity points
straight up and the pull points straight left, toward the sun. The position update moves the
planet along a straight line, up and off the curve, which leaves it a little farther from the sun,
so the potential energy rises. The velocity update adds a sideways kick at right angles to the
velocity, which makes the velocity longer, so the kinetic energy rises too. Both parts go up.
###

DT = 2.0 * pi / PER_ORBIT
after_one = 1.0 * START
euler_step(after_one, DT)
euler_one_step_gain = energy(after_one[0], after_one[1], after_one[2], after_one[3]) - start_energy
show DT
show euler_one_step_gain

###
The step is $\Delta t = 2\pi/200 \approx 0.0314$, and one Euler step from perihelion adds
$0.0496$ to the energy (`euler_one_step_gain`), a tenth of the $0.5$ that would set the planet
loose. Perihelion is where the planet moves fastest and the pull is strongest, so it is where a
step's error is largest; there are 2000 steps to come.

## Leapfrog kicks, drifts and kicks

*Leapfrog* does the same work per step, one evaluation of the force, in a different order. It
gives the velocity half a step's worth of acceleration (a *kick*), then moves the position a full
step with that updated velocity (a *drift*), then gives the velocity the other half kick using
the force at the new position:

$$\mathbf v_{n+\frac12} = \mathbf v_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf a(\mathbf r_n), \qquad
\mathbf r_{n+1} = \mathbf r_n + \Delta t\,\mathbf v_{n+\frac12}, \qquad
\mathbf v_{n+1} = \mathbf v_{n+\frac12} + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf a(\mathbf r_{n+1}).$$

The second kick's force is the next step's first kick's force, so a program that keeps it pays for
one force per step, the same as Euler. This one recomputes it, to keep each step on its own.
###

#| One leapfrog step of length dt on the state s = [x, y, vx, vy]: half a kick
#| to the velocity, a full drift of the position, and the other half kick with
#| the force at the new position.
def leapfrog_step(s: Arr, dt) {
    r3 = pow(s[0] * s[0] + s[1] * s[1], 1.5)
    s[2] = s[2] - 0.5 * dt * s[0] / r3
    s[3] = s[3] - 0.5 * dt * s[1] / r3
    s[0] = s[0] + dt * s[2]
    s[1] = s[1] + dt * s[3]
    r3 = pow(s[0] * s[0] + s[1] * s[1], 1.5)
    s[2] = s[2] - 0.5 * dt * s[0] / r3
    s[3] = s[3] - 0.5 * dt * s[1] / r3
    return 0.0
}

after_one_leap = 1.0 * START
leapfrog_step(after_one_leap, DT)
leap_one_step_change = energy(after_one_leap[0], after_one_leap[1], after_one_leap[2], after_one_leap[3]) - start_energy
show leap_one_step_change
# what ten orbits would add if every step erred the way this one did
leap_if_errors_added = ORBITS * PER_ORBIT * leap_one_step_change
show leap_if_errors_added
# how many times Euler's first step changes the energy more than leapfrog's
step_ratio = euler_one_step_gain / leap_one_step_change
show step_ratio

test "one Euler step changes the energy 398 times more than one leapfrog step" {
    # the prose states three digits
    assert_near(step_ratio, 398.0, 0.5)
}

###
From the same starting point, one leapfrog step changes the energy by $0.000125$
(`leap_one_step_change`), 398 times less than Euler's step (`step_ratio`). That is not yet the
difference that matters. If each of the 2000 steps added that much, ten orbits would add $0.25$
(`leap_if_errors_added`). What matters is whether the errors of many steps pile up or cancel.

## Running ten orbits

The next function runs either method for ten orbits and records the energy error
$|E - E_0|$, where $E_0 = -\tfrac12$ is the starting energy, at `SAMPLES` evenly spaced times.
It records the base-10 logarithm, because the errors range over many powers of ten and a
logarithm puts them on one readable scale; the $10^{-16}$ added inside keeps the logarithm finite
when the error is exactly zero. The planet's final state is left in `FINAL` for the checks further
down.
###

#| Integrate from perihelion and return log10 |E - E0| at SAMPLES times.
#| method 0 is forward Euler, 1 is leapfrog. FINAL gets the state at the end.
FINAL = zeros(len(START))
def energy_error(method, per_orbit) {
    dt = 2.0 * pi / per_orbit
    steps = ORBITS * per_orbit
    every = steps / SAMPLES
    s = 1.0 * START
    e0 = energy(s[0], s[1], s[2], s[3])
    out = zeros(SAMPLES)
    for n to steps {
        if method == 0.0 {
            euler_step(s, dt)
        }
        else {
            leapfrog_step(s, dt)
        }
        if mod(n + 1.0, every) == 0.0 {
            out[(n + 1.0) / every - 1.0] = log(abs(energy(s[0], s[1], s[2], s[3]) - e0) + 1.0e-16) / log(10.0)
        }
    }
    for k to len(s) {
        FINAL[k] = s[k]
    }
    return out
}

###
## Forward Euler, ten orbits

Before running: 2000 steps, each adding a little energy. Does the total reach the $0.5$ that
unbinds the planet?
###

YEARS = linspace(ORBITS / SAMPLES, ORBITS, SAMPLES)
euler = energy_error(0.0, PER_ORBIT)
euler_final = pow(10.0, euler[SAMPLES - 1.0])
euler_end = 1.0 * FINAL
euler_end_energy = energy(euler_end[0], euler_end[1], euler_end[2], euler_end[3])
show euler_final
show euler_end_energy

test "forward Euler has gained more than the binding energy 1/2: the planet is unbound" {
    assert_gt(euler_final, 0.5)
}

###
It does. After ten orbits Euler has added $0.546$ (`euler_final`), so the planet's energy is
$+0.046$ (`euler_end_energy`): positive, which means the simulated planet is no longer in orbit
at all. It is flying away. The real planet would go around forever.

## Leapfrog, ten orbits, same step

Before running: if leapfrog's errors simply added up, the $0.25$ from the cell above would be the
answer, half of what it takes to unbind the planet.
###

leap = energy_error(1.0, PER_ORBIT)
leap_worst = pow(10.0, max(leap))
leap_end = 1.0 * FINAL
show leap_worst
# the worst error as a share of the orbit's binding energy, 1/2
leap_worst_share = leap_worst / 0.5
show leap_worst_share

test "leapfrog's worst energy error is under one percent of the orbit's energy" {
    assert_lt(leap_worst, 0.01 * 0.5)
}
test "leapfrog's worst energy error is 0.74% of the orbit's energy" {
    # to the two digits the prose states
    assert_near(leap_worst_share, 0.0074, 0.00005)
}

###
The largest energy error leapfrog makes in ten orbits is $0.0037$ (`leap_worst`), which is
$0.74\%$ of the orbit's $0.5$ (`leap_worst_share`) and almost seventy times less than $0.25$. Its errors do not add up.

The figure shows both runs on a logarithmic scale. Before looking: Euler's error is largest
at perihelion, and the planet reaches perihelion once an orbit. Does Euler's error grow steadily,
or in jumps?
###

figure("Energy error over ten orbits, equal step size", "orbits", "$\\log_{10}$ of the energy error")
plot(YEARS, euler, "forward Euler")
plot(YEARS, leap, "leapfrog")

# Euler's error after the first orbit, and how long the orbit it put the planet
# on takes: a bound orbit with energy E has a = 1 / (2 |E|) and period a^(3/2)
euler_error_after_1_orbit = pow(10.0, euler[SAMPLES / ORBITS - 1.0])
euler_orbit_period = pow(1.0 / (2.0 * abs(start_energy + euler_error_after_1_orbit)), 1.5)
show euler_error_after_1_orbit
show euler_orbit_period
# leapfrog's worst error in the first orbit and in the tenth
leap_first_orbit = -20.0
leap_tenth_orbit = -20.0
for k to SAMPLES / ORBITS {
    leap_first_orbit = max(leap_first_orbit, leap[k])
    leap_tenth_orbit = max(leap_tenth_orbit, leap[SAMPLES - SAMPLES / ORBITS + k])
}
leap_first_orbit = pow(10.0, leap_first_orbit)
leap_tenth_orbit = pow(10.0, leap_tenth_orbit)
show leap_first_orbit
show leap_tenth_orbit
# leapfrog's typical error, the median of the samples, and the share of the
# samples that round to the same four decimals
leap_sorted = zeros(SAMPLES)
for k to SAMPLES {
    leap_sorted[k] = pow(10.0, leap[k])
}
sort(leap_sorted)
leap_median = 0.5 * (leap_sorted[SAMPLES / 2 - 1] + leap_sorted[SAMPLES / 2])
leap_near_median = 0.0
for k to SAMPLES {
    if abs(leap_sorted[k] - leap_median) < 0.00005 {
        leap_near_median = leap_near_median + 1.0
    }
}
leap_near_median = leap_near_median / SAMPLES
show leap_median
show leap_near_median

test "leapfrog's error sits near 0.0036 for most of each orbit" {
    assert_near(leap_median, 0.0036, 0.00005)
    # most: more than half of the samples are within 0.00005 of it
    assert_gt(leap_near_median, 0.5)
}

###
In jumps. Euler's error is $0.31$ after the first orbit (`euler_error_after_1_orbit`), nearly all
of it gained in the few steps around the starting perihelion. That leaves the planet on a larger
orbit, one that takes $4.3$ of the original orbits to go around (`euler_orbit_period`), so the
next close pass to the sun comes near orbit 4.3 on the plot. That pass adds the rest, the total
goes past $0.5$, and the planet leaves; there is no third pass.

Leapfrog's error sits near $0.0036$ for most of each orbit and dips as the planet swings past the
sun. Its worst in the first orbit is $0.0037$ (`leap_first_orbit`) and its worst in the tenth is
$0.0037$ (`leap_tenth_orbit`): the same level, nine orbits later.

## Why leapfrog's errors do not pile up

Leapfrog is *symplectic*. Each leapfrog step is the exact motion of a slightly different
system, one whose energy function differs from the true $E$ by an amount that shrinks with
$\Delta t^2$. The steps hold that modified energy almost exactly constant, so the true $E$ can
only wobble around it; it cannot drift away. Forward Euler has no such conserved quantity, so
each step's error is free to add to the last.

A second conserved quantity makes the same point more directly. The *angular momentum* per unit
mass, $L = x v_y - y v_x$, is constant for any force that points at the origin. At the start it is
$0.4 \times 2 = 0.8$, which equals $\sqrt{1 - e^2}$ for this orbit.

Before running: which method keeps $L$ at $0.8$? A leapfrog kick changes the velocity along
$\mathbf r$, and $\mathbf r \times \mathbf r = 0$, so a kick leaves $L$ alone. A drift changes the
position along $\mathbf v$, and $\mathbf v \times \mathbf v = 0$, so a drift leaves it alone too.
Leapfrog should keep $L$ to rounding error. Euler moves the position and the velocity at the same
time, from the old values; working out the product gives a change of $\Delta t^2 (v_x a_y - v_y
a_x)$ per step, which is not zero.
###

#| The angular momentum per unit mass of a state [x, y, vx, vy].
def angular_momentum(s: Arr) {
    return s[0] * s[3] - s[1] * s[2]
}

exact_momentum = sqrt(1.0 - ECC * ECC)
euler_momentum_drift = angular_momentum(euler_end) - exact_momentum
momentum_drift = abs(angular_momentum(leap_end) - exact_momentum)
show exact_momentum
show euler_momentum_drift
show momentum_drift

test "leapfrog keeps the angular momentum sqrt(1 - e^2) to rounding" {
    assert_lt(momentum_drift, 1.0e-12)
}

###
Euler's angular momentum has grown by $0.330$ (`euler_momentum_drift`), about two fifths of its
starting value. Leapfrog's drift is at the level of rounding error,
$2.9 \times 10^{-15}$ (`momentum_drift`), and the test holds it under $10^{-12}$.

## How the error shrinks with the step

A method is *order p* if its error shrinks like $\Delta t^p$: halve the step and the error drops
by a factor of $2^p$. Leapfrog is second order, so half the step should give a quarter of the
error. The cell below runs leapfrog again with 400 steps per orbit and measures $p$ from the two
worst errors:

$$p = \frac{\log_{10}(\text{error at } \Delta t) - \log_{10}(\text{error at } \Delta t/2)}{\log_{10} 2}.$$
###

FINE_PER_ORBIT = 2.0 * PER_ORBIT
leap_fine = energy_error(1.0, FINE_PER_ORBIT)
order = (max(leap) - max(leap_fine)) / (log(2.0) / log(10.0))
show order

test "and it is second order: half the step, a quarter of the error" {
    assert_near(order, 2.0, 0.1)
}

###
The measured order is $2.006$ (`order`). Twice the work per orbit buys four times the accuracy,
and the error stays bounded however long the run. Forward Euler is first order, and its error
keeps growing as the run gets longer.
###

posts.summaryHtml: Add more terms to the Fourier series of a square wave and the wiggle at the jump gets narrower, never shorter. It overshoots by 8.95% of the jump however many terms you take, and the number comes from an integral.
posts.summaryText: Add more terms to the Fourier series of a square wave and the wiggle at the jump gets narrower, never shorter. It overshoots by 8.95% of the jump however many terms you take, and the number comes from an integral.
notes: Take the square wave that is +1 on (0,π) and −1 on (−π,0). Its Fourier series is π4​(sinx+31​sin3x+51​sin5x+…): odd harmonics only, falling off like 1/k. Sum the first five and you get a wobbly approximation. Sum eighty and the wobble has all but gone — except right next to the jump, where a spike of the same height as ever has moved in toward x=0 and thinned.
[figure]
## Where the height comes from

The sum of the first m odd harmonics has its first peak at exactly x=π/2m, where the derivative π2​sin(2mx)/sinx first vanishes. Evaluate the sum there and it is a Riemann sum, with m panels, for π2​∫0π​tsint​dt=1.17898. So the height of the first peak tends to a number that has nothing to do with m: (2/π)Si(π), against a wave of height 1. The overshoot is 0.179, which is 8.95% of the jump from −1 to 1.
## Why more terms cannot help

The peak sits at π/2m and is about that wide, so as m grows it carries less and less area. In the mean-square sense the series converges: the integral of the squared error goes to zero. But at the peak itself the error stays 0.179 for every m. That is the difference between convergence in L2 and uniform convergence, and a square wave, being discontinuous, has the first without the second. A smoothing filter (Fejér, Lanczos) trades the spike for a slower approach to the wave; nothing that keeps the partial sums as they are removes it.
## What the program checks

The program checks three things. The peak of a thousand harmonics, summed directly, matches the integral computed by Simpson's rule with 2000 panels to a millionth. The peaks of ten and of a hundred harmonics are both above 1.17, so adding terms does not lower the peak. And the overshoot is 0.0895 of the jump, to four places.

pi = 3.141592653589793

#| The first m odd harmonics of a unit square wave, at the points x.
def partial_sum(x, m) {
    s = 0.0 * x
    for j to m {
        k = 2.0 * j + 1.0
        s = s + sin(k * x) / k
    }
    return (4.0 / pi) * s
}

#| The same sum at a single point x.
def partial_sum_at(x, m) {
    s = 0.0
    for j to m {
        k = 2.0 * j + 1.0
        s = s + sin(k * x) / k
    }
    return (4.0 / pi) * s
}

#| sin(t) / t, with its limit at zero.
def sinc(t) {
    if t == 0.0 {
        return 1.0
    }
    return sin(t) / t
}

limit = (2.0 / pi) * take the integral of sinc(t) from 0 to pi with 2000 intervals
peak_10 = partial_sum_at(pi / 20.0, 10.0)
peak_100 = partial_sum_at(pi / 200.0, 100.0)
peak_1000 = partial_sum_at(pi / 2000.0, 1000.0)
overshoot = (limit - 1.0) / 2.0
# how far the peak rises above the wave's height of 1
overshoot_height = limit - 1.0
show limit
show peak_10
show peak_100
show peak_1000
show overshoot
show overshoot_height

# The explanation, as an animation: the corner of the wave just after the jump at
# x = 0, one partial sum morphing into the next. The peak moves toward the jump and
# narrows; compare its height with the dashed line.
# points across the corner
NX = 220
X = linspace(0.0, 1.0, NX)
HARMONICS = [2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0, 80.0]

stage("Square wave at the jump, partial sums m = 5 to 80", 0.0, 1.0, 0.7, 1.25)
axes("x", "partial sum")
hline("wave", 1.0)
hline("limit", limit)
label("limit_name", "$\\tfrac{2}{\\pi}\\,\\mathrm{Si}(\\pi)$", 0.86, limit + 0.028)
curve("sum", X, partial_sum(X, 1.0))

fade_in("wave", 0.4)
say("the square wave is the dashed line at 1. One harmonic:")
draw("sum", 1.2)
wait(0.4)
for k to len(HARMONICS) {
    say("harmonics:", HARMONICS[k])
    morph("sum", X, partial_sum(X, HARMONICS[k]), 0.9)
    wait(0.35)
}
say("the peak has moved in and narrowed. Its height has not changed:")
together()
fade_in("limit", 0.6)
fade_in("limit_name", 0.6)
apart()
say("it sits at (2/pi) Si(pi) =", limit)
wait(1.2)

test "the peak of a thousand harmonics matches the integral (2/pi) Si(pi)" {
    assert_near(peak_1000, limit, 1.0e-6)
}
test "ten harmonics already overshoot by nearly as much: more terms do not help" {
    assert_gt(peak_10, 1.17)
    assert_gt(peak_100, 1.17)
}
test "the peak rises 0.179 above the wave" {
    # to the three digits the prose states
    assert_near(overshoot_height, 0.179, 0.0005)
}
test "the overshoot is 8.95% of the jump" {
    assert_near(overshoot, 0.0895, 1.0e-4)
}

functions.name: lyapunov
functions.what: The Lyapunov exponent at r: the orbit average of ln |f'(x)| = ln |r (1 - 2x)|.

posts.title: The logistic map at r = 4 has Lyapunov exponent ln 2
posts.titleHtml: The logistic map at r = 4 has Lyapunov exponent ln 2
posts.titleText: The logistic map at r = 4 has Lyapunov exponent ln 2
posts.summaryHtml: Iterate x→rx(1−x). At r=3.2 it settles on two values you can write down. At r=4 it never settles, nearby starts separate by a factor of two per step on average, and that factor is exact: the Lyapunov exponent is ln2.
posts.summaryText: Iterate x → r x(1 - x). At r = 3.2 it settles on two values you can write down. At r = 4 it never settles, nearby starts separate by a factor of two per step on average, and that factor is exact: the Lyapunov exponent is ln 2.
notes: At r=4, substitute x=sin2θ and the map becomes θ→2θ: angle doubling, which is where ln2 comes from. The two-cycle for 3<r<1+6​ solves f(f(x))=x with the fixed points divided out: x±​=(r+1±(r−3)(r+1)​)/2r.
posts.equationHtml: λ=n→∞lim​n1​k<n∑​ln∣r(1−2xk​)∣
posts.source:
# iterations discarded before the orbit is on its attractor: the transient
TRANSIENT = 500.0

#| The Lyapunov exponent at r: the orbit average of ln |f'(x)| = ln |r (1 - 2x)|.
def lyapunov(r, steps) {
    x = 0.3
    for s to TRANSIENT {
        x = r * x * (1.0 - x)
    }
    total = 0.0
    for s to steps {
        x = r * x * (1.0 - x)
        total = total + log(abs(r * (1.0 - 2.0 * x)))
    }
    return total / steps
}

# the attractor: for each r (a column), discard a transient, then count where the
# orbit goes (the rows, x = 1 at the top). Counts are capped so the two-cycle's
# two hot cells do not wash out the chaotic band.
NR = 160
NX = 100
KEEP = 240
# the transient discarded in each column of the picture
PICTURE_TRANSIENT = 400.0
R_LO = 2.8
visits = zeros(NX, NR)
for i to NR {
    r = R_LO + (4.0 - R_LO) * i / (NR - 1.0)
    x = 0.3
    for s to PICTURE_TRANSIENT {
        x = r * x * (1.0 - x)
    }
    for k to KEEP {
        x = r * x * (1.0 - x)
        row = NX - 1.0 - min(floor(x * NX), NX - 1.0)
        visits[row, i] = min(visits[row, i] + 1.0, 8.0)
    }
}

# the two-cycle at r = 3.2, reached by iterating, against its closed form
R2 = 3.2
# enough iterations for the orbit to settle on the two-cycle to the last digit
SETTLE = 2000.0
x = 0.3
for s to SETTLE {
    x = R2 * x * (1.0 - x)
}
reached_a = min(x, R2 * x * (1.0 - x))
reached_b = max(x, R2 * x * (1.0 - x))
root = sqrt((R2 - 3.0) * (R2 + 1.0))
exact_a = (R2 + 1.0 - root) / (2.0 * R2)
exact_b = (R2 + 1.0 + root) / (2.0 * R2)
chaos = lyapunov(4.0, 200000.0)
order = lyapunov(3.2, 20000.0)
show reached_a
show reached_b
show chaos
show order

figure("Attractor of x -> r x (1 - x), by r", "r", "x", 2.8, 4.0, 0.0, 1.0, "pixels")
plot2d(visits, "visits, capped at 8")

test "at r = 3.2 the orbit lands on the closed-form two-cycle" {
    assert_near(reached_a, exact_a, 1.0e-12)
    assert_near(reached_b, exact_b, 1.0e-12)
}
test "there the Lyapunov exponent is negative: nearby starts converge" {
    assert_lt(order, 0.0)
}
test "at r = 4 it is ln 2" {
    assert_near(chaos, log(2.0), 5.0e-3)
}

posts.summaryText: Put H = -1/2 ∂_x^2 + 1/2 x^2 on a grid and diagonalize: the levels come out at n + 1/2, a little low. How low is predictable. First-order perturbation theory gives -(h^2)/32(2n^2 + 2n + 1), and for the six lowest levels the measured shift matches it to within half a percent (the test allows 4%).
notes: The three-point second difference is ∂x2​+12h2​∂x4​+…, so the grid Hamiltonian is the true one plus −24h2​p4. To first order the level moves by the expectation of that, and for the oscillator ⟨n∣p4∣n⟩=43​(2n2+2n+1). The grid's error is a small perturbation of the Hamiltonian, so the perturbation theory used for the Stark shift predicts it.

posts.summaryHtml: Start just right of the cusp, at c=41​+ε, and count the steps of z→z2+c until z>2. Multiply the count by ε​. It tends to π.
posts.summaryText: Start just right of the cusp, at c = 1/4 + ε, and count the steps of z → z^2 + c until z > 2. Multiply the count by sqrt(ε). It tends to π.
notes: At c=41​ the map has a fixed point at z=21​ where its slope is exactly 1, and the orbit from z=0 climbs toward it in ever smaller steps without ever passing it. Raise c by ε and the fixed point disappears, but near z=21​ each step still moves z only a little. Write w=z−21​: each step is w→w+w2+ε, which for small steps is the differential equation dw/dn=w2+ε. The number of steps to get through is ∫−∞∞​dw/(w2+ε)=π/ε​.

posts.summaryText: Interpolate 1/(1 + 25x^2) by a polynomial through equally spaced points and the error grows as you add points. Move the same number of points to cos(jπ/n) and it falls geometrically, at a rate you can work out from where the function's poles are.
notes: The function has poles at x=±i/5. Polynomial interpolation in Chebyshev points converges like ρ−n, where ρ is the size of the largest ellipse with foci ±1 that the function is analytic inside. The ellipse through ±i/5 has ρ=51​+1+251​​=1.2198. Both interpolants use the barycentric formula, which is stable in Chebyshev points. With equally spaced points the problem is ill-conditioned (its Lebesgue constant grows exponentially with n), and this formula adds rounding error of its own.

posts.summaryHtml: Fill a symmetric 200×200 matrix with independent random numbers, divide by N​, and look at its eigenvalues. They do not scatter. They fill the semicircle 2π1​4−x2​, whatever distribution the entries came from.
posts.summaryText: Fill a symmetric 200 × 200 matrix with independent random numbers, divide by sqrt(N), and look at its eigenvalues. They do not scatter. They fill the semicircle 1/(2π)sqrt(4 - x^2), whatever distribution the entries came from.
notes: Only the entries' variance matters; these are uniform on [−3​,3​], which has variance 1 and looks nothing like a Gaussian. The even moments of the semicircle are the Catalan numbers 1,2,5,… because N1​TrH2k counts closed walks that never cross themselves. The tests check the second, fourth and sixth moments (1, 2 and 5), and that no eigenvalue lies beyond ±2.1.

At N=200 the program runs in your browser in about a tenth of a second. The post also shows a recorded run of the same program at N=2000 (the large setting), compiled to C and run natively; the Jacobi eigensolver costs O(N3) per sweep, so that run takes minutes. Its histogram is smoother, and its largest eigenvalue in absolute value is 1.996.

channels.summaryHtml: Numerical methods run on problems whose exact answer is known: floating-point arithmetic, time integrators, interpolation, Fourier sums, quadrature, eigenvalue solvers, matrix equations, partial differential equations and root finding. channels.title: Robotics
channels.summary: Systems that move, and the controllers that decide how. Each post writes out the dynamics and a controller and tests what the controller does in simulation; where an exact value exists (an equilibrium, an eigenvalue, a Riccati residual) it tests that too.
intro: Robotics research mostly benchmarks on simulators this site cannot run in a browser tab: MuJoCo locomotion (Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah, Ant, Humanoid), manipulation suites (Meta-World, robosuite, ManiSkill, RLBench, Franka Kitchen, Adroit), navigation (Habitat, AI2-THOR), and the large-scale trainers around them (Isaac Lab, Brax, MJX). The posts here cover what those simulators are built on: the equations they integrate, the classical controllers that learned policies are compared against, and tests that check both.
